title: WhatsApp Unveils Strict Parental Controls to Head Off Looming Age Laws
snippet: The new tools allow parents to customize rules about what their children see on the platform.
fullText:
WhatsApp announced in a blog post on Wednesday that it’s rolling out a new suite of parental controls to prevent teens from seeing content their parents may not want them to access.

The tools let parents choose who can see an underage user’s profile photo or invite those users to new groups. Parents can choose to receive notifications about significant group activity or changes. A similar set of controls lets parents limit how teens can use WhatsApp channels, what status updates they can see and who can see their status updates.

Parental controls are optional, and WhatsApp says they are simple to set up, requiring a single parent-set PIN. The controls can be adjusted or turned off at any time.

			

More from CNET

Controls also extend to Meta AI on WhatsApp, the app’s built-in chatbot, which offers a default setting for those 13 and up, and a strict, limited-content setting for younger children. WhatsApp says that personal messages and calls will always remain private, even from parents.

A representative for Meta, the owner of WhatsApp, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Parental controls weave carefully around age verification

Age verification and its data collection come with privacy concerns.FG Trade/Getty

WhatsApp is threading the needle here, attempting to satisfy growing demands for child protection while also avoiding heavy-handed age verification measures that can be both costly and unpopular with privacy advocates. We’ve already seen widespread age verification laws run into trouble in places like Australia, where a recent study shows platforms aren’t requiring proof of age. While WhatsApp is rolling out age verification for some features, it isn’t enforcing a platform-wide lockdown.

Determining whether someone is underage requires collecting personal information from everyone using the platform. Today’s age verification techniques often use uploaded images of driver’s licenses and passports, along with biometric face scans, which can end up in the hands of multiple companies and government bodies. Users can also circumvent the rules by using VPN services.

We recently saw Discord try a light form of age verification using vaguely explained criteria to assign its users presumed ages. Still, the company is running into bugs that sort users into the wrong age groups, errors which, as the Electronic Frontier Foundation points out, disproportionately affect minorities.

According to the Electronic Frontier Foundation, these privacy vulnerabilities and software bugs mirror the core flaws of the Kids Online Safety Act, a controversial bill currently advancing through Congress. This bill imposes various age verification requirements on online platforms while attempting to define prohibited content, which ranges from articles referencing alcohol to guides concerning sexual activity.

WhatsApp is taking a different path, offering more powerful parental controls as an alternative for worried families, potentially showing them that age-verification laws aren’t necessary.

Are parental controls safer than age verification?

The safety of parental controls depends on the user’s priorities. Technically, parental controls on phones, routers and platforms like WhatsApp can provide all the protection that age verification systems offer. Still, parents have to monitor and configure the controls themselves, adjusting the guidelines as children age.

One faction prefers to put the controls in the hands of the online platforms and the governments that regulate them, which saves them time and tough choices. Another faction views this as a dangerous risk to personal privacy and as an increase in social surveillance.

To keep track of verification laws and how they affect privacy, you can consult this online tool from the Free Speech Coalition, which tracks current age verification laws by state.

title: Google thinks SpaceX’s Starship has to launch 1,800 times before space data centers get off the ground
snippet: Google launched its first advanced chip into orbit to pave the way for space data centers.
fullText:
Google’s prototype of its orbital compute satellite took off today onboard a SpaceX rocket launched from California — the first time the tech giant has sent one of its advanced chips into space.

Built by Planet Labs, the satellite will prove that a Google Tensor Processing Unit, its competitor to Nvidia’s GPUs, can function in space. That means supplying a kilowatt of continuous power, cooling the chip, and running a series of models through their paces to see if anything goes wrong.

“We’ve done testing on the ground, but you know, there’s no test that’s completely as good as the real thing,” said Travis Beals, the Google executive managing Project Suncatcher, the tech giant’s plan to develop large-scale compute clusters in orbit around the Earth.

Once commissioned, the satellite will fire up its TPU in 15-minute bursts to avoid straining the satellite’s power and thermal management systems. This satellite is based on a standard platform built by Planet Labs, but the two companies are working on a demo expected to take flight next year that will see two satellites more purpose-built for advanced compute that can run more substantial workloads. Those future versions will attempt to collaborate via a laser communications link.

Suncatcher isn’t the only space AI payload on this SpaceX rocket, which is launching more than 100 different payloads, including missions from Satlyt and Cowboy Space Company.

What sets the Google initiative apart from those startups (and indeed from SpaceX itself) is that it’s a long-term project. 

The focus of this “long-term moonshot,” as Beals puts it, is on building for the space infrastructure and AI workloads that will exist in the future. The company envisions an orbital data center that is a network of 81 satellites flying in close formation, processing in parallel.

“The bandwidth and the latency between TPUs really, really matters when you’re trying to run a multi-rack workload…we’re trying to look ahead to not just what workloads exist today, but where they will be in five years,” Beals said. That’s largely because the rockets required to scale up orbital data centers in a cost-effective way don’t yet exist. 

On Thursday, Google also released a peer-reviewed version of its white paper on orbital data centers, one of the most rigorous analyses available of how compute gets to orbit. The paper will be published in Joule.

One of the paper’s most notable aspects is how Google thinks about access to space. Although the researchers stress their analysis isn’t an economic feasibility study, it offers an interesting picture of how the company sees rockets becoming cheaper over time. 

Like all data center companies, Google is looking to SpaceX to get its spacecraft off the ground. (Google is also a major investor in SpaceX.) 

Arguing that Elon Musk’s rocket builders have achieved a price-reducing “learning curve” of about 20% a year since they launched the Falcon 1 rocket, the authors believe it’s reasonable to expect the company to deliver launch prices close to $200 per kilogram by 2035.

What will it take to do that? Based on the amount of payload launched by the Falcon 9, they think a similar cost-reduction trajectory will require Starship to fly 370,000 tons of payload into orbit. That’s something that would take it about 1,800 launches over the next 10 years, or 180 a year — and that’s if it can fly 200 metric tons on each mission.

That’s a big ask for a vehicle that has never flown more than five times in a year. SpaceX predicts the company will be flying far more than that — Elon Musk has suggested Starship could achieve an hourly flight rate in 2029, for example, but Musk says a lot of things.

The good news, at least, in Google’s updated research, is that it seems likely that its chips will survive the radiation of space. The company had to redo tests blasting the chips in a particle accelerator after they realized the configuration of the chips provided more shielding than they would actually experience. This produced slightly more errors in the chip’s logic circuitry, but the company is still confident its chips can handle large inference workloads in orbit for the five-year lifespan of a satellite.

“The error rate is very low if you’re thinking about typical inference operations, right? Like one in a million,” Beals said. “On the other hand, it was already problematic for doing, say, some mega-scale training run where you’re going to have many thousands of chips running for months.”

Correction: The headline for this story originally misstated the learning curve estimate for Starship launches as 1,600; it is 1,800.

title: Opus 5.5 loves to tell you ‘this matters’ (and other AI writing tells)
snippet: Opus 5.5’s biggest tell is the word “dependable,” which pops up 23 times more often than in human samples.
fullText:
Now that LLM-generated prose is everywhere, human beings are eager for ways to sniff it out. While early tells like em-dashes and “delve” are long gone, researchers say there are still plenty of telltale habits that AI models fall back on when writing prose.

A new study from the marketing firm Graphite looked at the writing habits of frontier models, sussing out each model’s favorite words and phrases. While old tells like em-dash use have been stamped out, models still fall back on contrast-heavy constructions, with each model version showing its own unique quirks. The biggest surprise is how broad the scope of tells turns out to be. Graphite found 13,000 phrases that were at least twice as common in the AI content as human content — their definition of a “tell.” 

“It turns out that Claude models are actually getting closer to the human word distribution over time,” Graphite’s chief AI officer Greg Druck told TechCrunch. “And for the GPT models, it’s getting further away.”

Studying AI-generated writing at scale required a careful study design. Graphite started with a corpus of 10,000 articles published before the release of ChatGPT, serving as the human-generated control group. Then researchers had different AI models rewrite the articles from summaries, hoping to eliminate as much source bias as possible. With matching samples from both humans and each model, they could compare how often certain words and phrases appeared in AI writing, as well as broader patterns in sentence construction.

According to Graphite’s results, Claude Opus 5.5’s biggest tell is the word “dependable,” which pops up 23 times more often than in human samples. While Opus 5.5 now avoids the “it’s not X, it’s Y” sentence construction, it still tends to say something “is more than an X, it’s a Y.” 

Above all, Opus loves to tell you why things matter, using the phrase “this matters” 116 times more often than human writing, while “why X matters” occurs 92 times more often.

OpenAI’s Astra has a different set of tip-offs. This model loves to describe “another dimension” of whatever it’s talking about, and tends to hedge claims by saying an action “may provide” or “can provide” a particular benefit. Its biggest tell is what Graphite calls the “corrective framing,” where a topic is defined as “not simply X” or offered as an alternative, “rather than relying on X.” According to graphite’s research, those constructions were more than 100 times more common in Astra-generated prose than in human writing.

Notably, all the frontier labs seem to have responded to the idea that models overuse em-dashes. In Graphite’s samples, Opus 5.5 used the punctuation mark 99% less often than Opus 5. Astra now uses it 88% less than human samples, whereas Gemini 3.1 Pro has almost completely eliminated the em-dash from its writing.

But while individual tells change, Graphite says the overall number is mostly holding steady. “It’s not like the tells are decreasing,” Druck told TechCrunch. “They are managing to remove the most well-known tells, but other ones pop up. And every model version has its own.”

It’s surprising that tells are so persistent, given the labs’ focus on human-like writing styles. In the Opus 5.5 release, Anthropic boasted that the model “communicates more naturally than prior models,” saying early users “found its writing clearer and easier to follow.”

OpenAI made similar claims when releasing the GPT-6 versions of Sol and Luna, saying users could “expect to see more clarity, less jargon, [and] fewer odd turns of phrase.”

But Druck is skeptical about how much the labs can do to completely eliminate telltale construction or phrases.

“A general hypothesis I have is that the labs are less able to control some of these things than you might expect,” Druck says. “These are giant models with billions of parameters. They have some finite number of tests they can run, and things slip through.”

title: Lenovo’s first Googlebook actually costs $200 less than announced, and it’s not the only one
snippet: Lenovo today put a spotlight on its Googlebook release, also confirming that initial pricing was incorrect and that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 will, in fact, start at $1,099. more…
fullText:
Lenovo today put a spotlight on its Googlebook release, also confirming that initial pricing was incorrect and that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 will, in fact, start at $1,099.

The Lenovo Googlebook 15 is one of the first five machines running the new Googlebook OS which replaces ChromeOS. This is designed for “professionals, creators, and business owners,” Lenovo said in a press release:

Powered by Intel Core Ultra 5 processors with built-in Gemini Intelligence, up to 32GB of memory and up to 512GB of storage, the Lenovo Googlebook 15 helps users stay productive and connected – no matter where the day takes them.

Designed for professionals, creators and business owners, the Lenovo Googlebook 15 delivers up to 47 TOPS of performance while weighing under 3 lbs., making it the lightest 15-inch device in Lenovo’s portfolio.

It’s certainly a workhorse, with core specs including a 15-inch OLED 120Hz refresh rate, Intel Core Ultra 5 processors, up to 32GB of RAM, and up to 512GB of storage. Lenovo also touts a haptic trackpad, 12.5-hour battery life, top-facing Dolby Atmos speakers, a metal chassis, and Lenovo even built a wireless mouse with a matching “Glowbar” for the Googlebook platform.

And it’s cheaper than we first thought.

	

Google initially announced that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 would start at $1,299, but Lenovo has now confirmed it actually starts at $1,099. That’s for the model with 16GB of RAM, 512GB of storage, and a Core Ultra 5 chip. Google Store, for some reason, still lists the machine at $1,149, but Best Buy has the correct pricing. 

	

Lenovo says its Googlebook, like others, will be available starting on October 4.

This isn’t the only model where Google messed up the intial pricing announcement. The Dell XPS Googlebook was initially announced at a starting price of $1,199, but is actually $999.

These probably aren’t a result of feedback on the high overall pricing – Best Buy was always showing the correct prices, so this was only on Google’s end – but Google hasn’t publicly acknowledged exactly what’s going on. For those actually looking to buy a Googlebook, though, lower prices are great news. Asus and HP’s Googlebooks still start at $1,299, while the Acer Googlebook is the most affordable of the lot at $899.

title: Here’s how many iPhone Duo units Apple is reportedly making
snippet: A recent report from Chinese outlet Jiemian News offers an update on iPhone Duo production, including how many units are being made, assembly troubles, and more. more…
fullText:
A recent report from Chinese outlet Jiemian News offers an update on iPhone Duo production, including how many units are being made, assembly troubles, and more.

Latest iPhone Duo report covers production struggles, target inventory, and more

iPhone Duo goes up for pre-order on October 16, just a little more than two weeks from now. And a recent report from Jiemian News provides the latest update on Apple’s production status.

We’ve seen reporting before that Apple’s foldable is having a slow ramp-up due to a complex assembly process. 

Right now, iPhone Duo assembly yield is reportedly just over 60%. And per Jiemian, suppliers believe it could take another six months or more for production yields to reach a “mature” level.

That’s far below what would be expected for other models, but perhaps not surprising considering the Duo is packed with all-new product designs and components.

Per the report, Apple is targeting having 6-8 million iPhone Duo units ready to go for 2026. This compares to 20-30 million typical units for a flagship new Pro or Pro Max model.

	

With a starting price of $1,999 and unique form factor, iPhone Duo isn’t targeting as broad a set of users as models like iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The overall foldable market is still fairly niche, too. 

If Apple sells anywhere near 8 million units before the end of 2026, that will no doubt be seen as a major win. But the iPhone Duo’s success will ultimately come down more to popularity over time. Will it be an early adopter model only, or prove a mass-market hit too?

A source told Jiemian that Apple so far has been unwilling to relax its strict quality standards for the iPhone Duo, thus leading to lower than expected yields. While that potentially will lead to shortages when the new model launches, I suspect anyone spending $2,000+ on an iPhone will want the highest quality product, so it’s not exactly bad news.

title: Bank of America says Meta’s Muse highlights a new risk for Apple’s services revenue
snippet: In a new investor note issued today, Bank of America says Meta’s new Muse AI agent highlights how third-party AI agents could increasingly bypass Apple’s ecosystem and threaten its services revenue. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new investor note issued today, Bank of America says Meta’s new Muse AI agent highlights how third-party AI agents could increasingly bypass Apple’s ecosystem and threaten its services revenue. Here are the details.

BofA maintains “Buy” rating

Apple’s shares dropped more than 2.5% today, after Bank of America’s Wamsi Mohan issued an investor note warning that AI agents such as Meta’s Muse could increasingly capture product discovery, referrals, and transactions that currently take place through Apple’s ecosystem.

From his note, via SeekingAlpha:

“The risk for Apple is that it can keep every handset sale and still lose discovery, referral, and transaction initiation.”

Mohan’s note comes as Meta’s Muse nears two weeks at No. 1 on the US App Store’s free apps chart. According to Sensor Tower estimates cited by TechCrunch, Muse has amassed more than 3.4 million downloads as of last week.

Meta’s OpenClaw-like AI agent can browse the web, fill out forms, book trips, send emails, and make purchases on a user’s behalf, and it seems to have caught on with the general public, as it took just 10 days to overtake ChatGPT at the top of the US App Store.

Back to Mohan’s note, he maintained a “Buy” rating and $370 price target on Apple, arguing that despite the new risks posed by AI agents, he still sees the company as an “eventual winner of AI at the edge.”

From his note, via Yahoo! Finance:

“Whomever the agent chooses becomes the merchant, and whoever owns the agent collects the routing economics that previously accrued to operating systems, search, and app stores.”

Mohan also points to Muse’s growing list of commerce integrations, including Shopify and Shop Pay, Expedia, and PayPal, as examples of how AI agents can increasingly handle transactions from discovery through checkout.

Additionally, Mohan notes that modern iPhones already have more than enough computing power to run AI agents, making software execution and integration the bigger challenge for Apple.

In his note, Mohan argues that Apple needs its Services, silicon, payments, privacy, and Siri AI teams to move together more quickly if the company wants to compete for what he calls the “economics of user intent.”

	

Specifically on Siri AI, he also noted that it lacks some of Muse’s capabilities, including persistent background tasks, broad third-party action support, and a dedicated agent payment rail.

He also pointed out the difference in development pace, with Apple typically shipping major software updates once a year, while AI agents can “improve daily.”

That said, Mohan sees Apple’s massive installed base and reputation for privacy as important advantages, particularly when it comes to convincing users to trust AI agents with sensitive tasks.

title: Some Pixel models reportedly experiencing an NFC bug that breaks contactless payments
snippet: Following several Pixel 11-specific bugs after the phone’s launch, another one reportedly breaks NFC tap-to-pay, used for contactless payments. But this one is affecting more than just the Pixel 11. more…
fullText:
Following several Pixel 11-specific bugs after the phone’s launch, another one reportedly breaks NFC tap-to-pay, used for contactless payments. But this one is affecting more than just the Pixel 11.

A slew of reports on Reddit have been posted within the last two weeks regarding a new Google Pixel bug that affects NFC payments (via Android Authority). Users have been reporting that their Pixel devices can no longer use tap-to-pay, whether directly in the Google Wallet app or at automatic transit terminals that don’t require the app to be open.

The issue isn’t affecting just the Pixel 11, so this can’t be piled onto the list of device-specific issues users are coming across – of which there are a good few. The Reddit posts and comments within list Google Pixel models ranging from the Pixel 8 to the new Pixel 11 Pro XL. The bug is agnostic to model or series, given it’s still supported.

	

The obvious response, noted by more than a few commenters, suggests using the Pixel 11 correctly. The NFC antenna is placed slightly higher than on other models, so the first suggestion appears to be “move your phone” to solve the Google Pixel’s NFC bug.

	

Of course, this would only apply if the Pixel 11’s NFC antenna were alone in experiencing this bug. Because it isn’t, it’s easier to point at a software update that made NFC unusable with Google Wallet. Some users note NFC still works in other functions, but not with payments.

Google has yet to respond, it seems. That doesn’t mean the company isn’t aware of the Pixel bug, but it might suggest users will need to wait a little longer for a fix. That being said, loss of tap-to-pay is a pretty big deal for a phone in 2026.

fullText:
Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison has announced that the company will just be called Skydance when it completes its $110 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery next week. In a post on X, Ellison writes that “we wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. — and all our extraordinary brands — to remain in the spotlight.”

Earlier this week, a judge approved the settlement Paramount reached with California and 11 other states that sued over the planned acquisition, clearing the last major hurdle blocking the deal. Under the deal, Paramount must release a minimum number of theatrical films over the next five years, starting with 30 annually in years one and two.

Ahead of the close, Paramount has also appointed Ynon Kreiz, the former chairman and CEO of Mattel, as the co-CEO of the soon-to-be even bigger company. The deal is expected to close on October 6th.

Here’s Ellison’s full announcement:

What once was the peak, is now just the beginning.

Paramount and Warner Bros. shaped over a century of culture. By combining them, we aren’t rewriting history — we’re equipping these iconic studios with a more powerful engine. Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for bold, quality storytelling.

We chose this name for a few important reasons. First and foremost, as we bring Paramount and Warner Bros. together, we wanted to preserve what has made each of these studios iconic. Both have distinct identities, extraordinary legacies and brands that have resonated with audiences for generations. We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one. Instead, we wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. — and all our extraordinary brands — to remain in the spotlight.

We have big goals for Skydance, and we intend to pursue them with passion, imagination and a willingness to take smart risks. At the same time, we will honor what makes Paramount and Warner Bros. special — giving both studios the opportunity to grow, tell more great stories and bring those stories to even broader audiences around the world, powered by the scale and capabilities of Skydance.

I couldn’t be more excited about what we’re going to build together.

title: Rivian’s R2 just helped it set a new sales record
snippet: Deliveries jumped roughly 45% compared to the same quarter last year, with Rivian delivering more than 19,000 EVs.
fullText:
Rivian sold more electric vehicles than ever in the third quarter, thanks in large part to the launch of its new, more affordable R2 SUV. 

The company said Friday morning that it built 19,751 vehicles and delivered 19,248. That’s roughly 45% more than it delivered in the same period last year. 

While Rivian didn’t break out how many of those were R2 SUVs, this was the first full quarter of sales of the new vehicle after it launched in June. The company said Friday that it will release its full third-quarter financial results on October 29.

Rivian has big plans for the R2, which currently starts at just under $60,000. The company is betting that it will sell between 20,000 to 25,000 R2 vehicles by the end of the year, which would make it one of the fastest-selling EVs in U.S. history — second only to Tesla’s Model Y. Rivian also plans to make cheaper models available that will cost as low as around $45,000.

If Rivian hits those numbers, the company believes it can sell between 65,000 and 70,000 vehicles this year, including its R1 lineup of vehicles and its commercial electric van. That would be its best sales year ever, as the company has spent the last few years stuck at around the 50,000-vehicles-sold mark. 

Rivian is currently building the R2 at its factory in Normal, Illinois, where it recently expanded the production space to accommodate the new SUV. But Rivian is also building a brand new factory outside Atlanta, Georgia, where it expects to be able to build as many as 300,000 vehicles per year in the near future, with the option to expand that capacity down the road. 

Rivian needs the R2 to sell well in order to staunch years of heavy losses, due in part to the company’s expensive infrastructure required to support this mass-market vehicle. But Rivian has also signed a deal with Uber to make robotaxi versions of the R2 SUV. Rivian believes robotaxis represent such a big potential market that, in March, the company pushed back its goal of reaching profitability in 2027 to invest more money into autonomy.

title: Home Assistant says ‘Big tech ruined the cloud, so we’re out’
snippet: Home Assistant is renaming its cloud service to Home Assistant Link and removing the cloud from its logo. | Image: Nabu Casa The open-source smart home platform Home Assistant is kicking the cloud to the curb - in name at least. "We are renaming Home Assistant Cloud to Home Assistant Link, because we hate clouds," founder Paulus Schoutsen told The Verge in an interview ahead of today's announcement. "Big tech ruined the cloud, so we're out." The move is part of a long-term strategy Schoutsen and his team have been pursuing to make Home Assistant a mainstream smart home platform. Schoutsen says most users find the powerful platform after hitting the limits of mainstream options like Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Apple Home. But it has a steep learning curve, and … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
The open-source smart home platform Home Assistant is kicking the cloud to the curb — in name at least. “We are renaming Home Assistant Cloud to Home Assistant Link, because we hate clouds,” founder Paulus Schoutsen told The Verge in an interview ahead of today’s announcement. “Big tech ruined the cloud, so we’re out.”

The move is part of a long-term strategy Schoutsen and his team have been pursuing to make Home Assistant a mainstream smart home platform. Schoutsen says most users find the powerful platform after hitting the limits of mainstream options like Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Apple Home. But it has a steep learning curve, and that’s what he’s looking to change.

I spoke with Schoutsen at the Z-Wave Summit in Boca Raton, Florida, this week about the changes and Home Assistant’s future plans, which include lowering barriers to entry by developing simpler dashboards, making setup more intuitive, and using generative AI to reduce complexity. He also said they plan to launch a new hub next year that’s more user-friendly. “We’re growing up.”

“You don’t have to trust me not to misuse your data because I just don’t have your data.”

— Paulus Schoutsen

Renaming Home Assistant Cloud to Link is mostly symbolic. The features stay the same, aside from some back-end improvements to speed and reliability. The new name also tries to address a concern some new users had that it meant Home Assistant ran in the cloud, says Schoutsen. Home Assistant runs on local hardware and controls your smart home locally, but this means once you leave your home network, you can’t control anything.

For $6.50 a month or $65 a year, Home Assistant Link gives you a convenient way to access your Home Assistant instance from anywhere, alongside the option to enable other internet-dependent features such as integration with Alexa and Google voice control, text-to-speech, speech-to-text, and encrypted backups.

The move addresses an awkward dynamic for the platform. Schoutsen and his team have spent years campaigning against proprietary cloud ecosystems, which he believes hurt the smart home, and encouraging people not to buy cloud-dependent products, all while offering a service with “cloud” in the name. However, unlike some cloud services, Home Assistant Cloud was never mandatory, and you could always replicate everything it provided with other methods; the same remains true for Link.

Schoutsen says Link is also different from many cloud services because it has no access to your data. Link is run by Nabu Casa, Home Assistant’s commercial partner, and all Link traffic is encrypted. “We can’t see it, and we don’t want to,“ he says. “You don’t have to trust me not to misuse your data because I just don’t have your data.” The service provides a revenue stream to fund the platform’s development, with 60 percent of the profit going to the non-profit Open Home Foundation that runs Home Assistant.

For Home Assistant, cloud-dependent products are a hard no. “The cloud is ruining how people think of the smart home,” says Schoutsen, pointing to the recent examples of Nest shutting off the cloud for its early thermostats, smart TVs sending your data to the cloud without you knowing, and Weber sunsetting the June Oven’s servers. “Now you have a dumb oven that cost $1,500. It’s crazy,” he says. “People get so used to it and get so disappointed by it.”

The cloud isn’t all bad, Schoutsen concedes. Speech-to-text, backups, and AI work better online, but the problem is products that stop working without it. He wants product manufacturers to commit to offering local control by default, using open standards (Matter, Zigbee, Z-Wave, MQTT, ESPHome), never locking basic features behind a cloud, and allowing users to control their own data.

“I’d love to see a nutrition label on boxes showing if a product is cloud-dependent or not,” he says, adding that they’re building a database to help consumers find products that aren’t fully reliant on the cloud.

This stance against the cloud is likely to appeal to consumers who are increasingly concerned about who has access to their data. But Home Assistant still has a long way to go before it becomes mainstream. Schoutsen says Home Assistant is installed in an estimated 2.7 million homes, but that’s still a fraction of the reach of Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Samsung SmartThings, and Apple Home. Winning over mainstream users will be hard.

The biggest barrier to entry is complexity. Home Assistant does a lot, meaning you have a lot of choice, which can be overwhelming. “If you want to try something with Home Assistant, the answer is never no,” says Schoutsen. “We want everything to be possible, which means that the UX is more complicated, and that scares people.” In comparison, “You open Apple Home, and there’s like nothing you can do,” he says.

Over the last few years, the team has been working to remove those barriers without taking away functionality. “We’re looking to lower the floor without lowering the ceiling,” he says. There are plans to launch a successor to the Home Assistant Green hub that will be easier to set up. “We want to make it more like onboarding a Philips Hue hub,” says Schoutsen.

They are also working to make the UX easier and will integrate the HACS community store — where users find and install community-built integrations — into Home Assistant next month. This should make integrations easier to find and set up. “If people haven’t tried Home Assistant in over a year, they should give it a shot,” he says.

“We’re looking to lower the floor without lowering the ceiling.”

— Paulus Schoutsen

Another big push that could turn into a major selling point for the platform is a “No Device Left Behind” program. Nabu Casa is developing devices that will more easily bring people’s existing analog or legacy tech into the platform — such as old receivers, AC units, solar panel inverters, even TVs — using technology such as serial, IR, and Modbus.

Schoutsen sees AI as a big driver for Home Assistant. “AI is going to solve the complexity problem, and our biggest weakness is becoming our biggest strength,” he says. As a broad, open platform that can bring together data and controls from across your smart home, Home Assistant could provide a useful foundation for AI agents.

I used Claude to set up Home Assistant last year, and it was a big improvement over trying to figure out what on earth YAML was. “Soon you’re just going to have your agent configure your software for you,” he says. “Because people don’t want the software, they just want the solution that comes out of it.” Schoutsen acknowledges that agents raise obvious privacy concerns, but says Home Assistant keeps your data at home and you can choose which agent to trust with it, including one that runs locally.

Ultimately, Home Assistant may not need to reinvent itself to win over the mainstream if it can become the foundational layer that lets your home talk to your AI agent or platform of choice. “If you just have a box in your house that runs Home Assistant that connects all your data to your agents or to, say, Apple Home, that’s great,” he says. “That’s a win for Home Assistant.”

Nearly twelve years to the day after Apple first announced Apple Pay, the feature is now rolling out in India, one of the few major markets where it had yet to become available. fullText:
Update, 10:13 p.m. ET: Apple has now confirmed the launch for “customers with Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard credit cards.” The original story follows below.

Nearly twelve years to the day after Apple first announced Apple Pay, the feature is now rolling out in India, one of the few major markets where it had yet to become available. Here are the details.

Apple Pay finally expanding to India

Earlier today, TechCrunch reported that Apple Pay would launch in India “later Tuesday with Axis Bank as its initial banking partner.”

Now, as spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple has begun enabling Apple Pay support in India on its servers, suggesting the rollout is officially underway.

According to an Apple support article, there are now 101 countries and regions that support Apple Pay, including India.

India has quickly become one of the most strategically important countries for Apple, both in terms of manufacturing and consumer growth.

In addition to expanding its retail presence and repeatedly highlighting strong growth in the country during quarterly earnings calls, Apple and its suppliers have been shifting more iPhone production to India as part of a broader effort to diversify manufacturing beyond China.

That expansion has not been without its controversies. Apple is currently fighting an antitrust case brought by the Competition Commission of India over its App Store practices, and the company has also refused to comply with a government order requiring smartphone makers to preinstall a state-run app on new devices.

Apple manufacturing partner Tata Electronics has also recently come under fire after an Indian pollution regulator alleged that wastewater from one of its iPhone component factories contaminated groundwater and nearby farmland.

Tata was also recently targeted by a cyberattack that allegedly exposed confidential files from several companies, including Apple.

All of that said, Apple’s launch of Apple Pay in India signals another step in the company’s broader expansion in the country and comes at a potentially useful time for its Services business.

During the last fiscal quarter, Apple saw its first sequential drop in Services revenue since fiscal Q4 2022. Of course, India is unlikely to move that needle on its own, but with iPhone sales reaching record levels in the country, Apple Pay gives the company another way to keep building on that momentum.

title: Musk’s AI chatbot Grok reportedly encouraged Trump to capture Venezuela’s president
snippet: President Trump reportedly asked for Grok's opinion before invading Venezuela and capturing Nicolás Maduro.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

2:08 PM PDT · October 1, 2026

Image Credits:Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

In December 2025, about a month before the U.S. invaded Venezuela and captured its president, Nicolás Maduro, President Trump had a secret meeting with Elon Musk, Time magazine reports. This was roughly seven months after Musk left his role in the Trump administration at the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

During this meeting, Trump “spent hours” talking to Musk’s Grok chatbot, including asking how Venezuelans would respond to the capture of their president, a source told Time. Just a few months earlier, in September, Trump began ordering U.S. military strikes against Venezuelan boats that Trump alleged were involved in drug trafficking.

People had apparently been turning to Grok asking about the boat strikes and political climate in Venezuela, as The Atlantic reported at the time. So Grok told Trump that Maduro was a “deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall,” Time reported.

When such celebrations indeed happened after the U.S. invaded on January 3, Trump apparently “came away thinking Grok was ingenious,” that source told Time.

So perhaps it should come as no surprise that in June of this year, the Pentagon’s head of AI said that the military used Grok Gov to deploy and strike targets during the Iran War.

While Grok isn’t the only AI model serving the DoD (OpenAI also has an agreement and Anthropic has been in a back-and-forth over how its models can be used for military intelligence and in modern warfare), Grok may become an even bigger favorite under this administration. Earlier this week, the Pentagon announced that Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey have been tapped to co-lead a study about how advanced technology is, and can be, used in battlefields.

title: Amazon Delivery Driver Smart Glasses Will Snap Pictures of… Everything?
snippet: As Amazon continues its rollout of AI smart glasses, privacy concerns are growing.
fullText:
A few days ago, I crossed paths with an Amazon delivery driver who was wearing some odd-looking glasses. I paused, wondering if it was a pair of the new AI smart glasses (I reported on them last year) or if he just had questionable taste in eyewear. After Wednesday’s news, my curiosity has evolved into concern.

In a Bloomberg opinion piece, reporter Dave Lee shared his thoughts on the new AI smart glasses based on an interview with Amazon executive Viraj Chatterjee, who is spearheading the rollout. According to the report, Amazon aims to have 5,000 drivers wearing the glasses by the end of 2026, expanding to more than 20,000 by the end of 2027.

The e-commerce giant says the new AI smart glasses will track a driver’s shift from beginning to end to ensure quicker, more reliable deliveries, reduce errors and streamline delivery by giving drivers hands-free guidance. But Bloomberg’s Lee said that “the company is sleepwalking into yet another invasion-of-privacy furor.”

			

More from CNET

While a driver is on foot, the glasses capture static photos of everything in their line of sight at a high frequency (likely every few seconds), generating thousands of photos per shift. These images, which will include package recipients, people on the street and private property, will be handed off to real-life human employees at Amazon for analysis. The captured photos will then be fed into Amazon’s Wellspring, the company’s generative AI platform used to map neighborhoods and improve the accuracy of delivery locations.

Privacy red flags appear to be everywhere, compounded by Chatterjee telling Bloomberg that customer opt-out options haven’t even been considered.

Amazon spokesperson Leigh Anne Gullett disputed Bloomberg’s reporting, saying, “The suggestion that Amazon is using smart delivery glasses as a surveillance tool fundamentally mischaracterizes the technology and its purpose.” Gullett told CNET that Amazon continues to incorporate feedback during the pilot period and that participation is voluntary for delivery partners and drivers.

Amazon is developing AI-powered smart glasses to help streamline work for its delivery drivers.

Amazon

Surveillance and regimentation

When pressed on the idea of these smart glasses cameras being used for surveillance, Chatterjee explained to Bloomberg that the images will be blurred before human reviewers see them if they contain identifying information, such as a license plate or a face. 

Gullett told CNET that privacy protections have been built into the technology from the beginning and that the technology features automatic data blurring, strict access controls and a physical hardware privacy switch.

But still, a lot of us will be kept in the dark. There seems to be no way for you, as the Amazon customer, to know whether these types of images even exist, as there reportedly won’t be a way to view them or request their deletion. According to the Bloomberg report, the only real way to pull up those images is to serve a warrant.

There’s also the added vulnerability of these AI devices to hacking. Given that the content may contain personally identifiable information, Amazon would be tasked with establishing strict guardrails to prevent sensitive data from falling into the wrong hands. 

The smart glasses rollout also raises critical concerns regarding the regimentation of the workforce. Amazon delivery vans already use cameras and sensors to monitor driving habits and cabin behavior. If glasses track a driver’s exact movements on foot, that would create a virtually continuous log of their shift. Drivers often report that data collected under the guise of “safety and efficiency” is used to monitor performance, dock pay or penalize them.

In the Amazon driver subreddit, workers note that the company prioritized funding this AI smart glasses rollout over fair raises or basic workplace necessities — like time for real bathroom breaks rather than using plastic bottles. The rollout has also intensified fears that the company intends to use its AI infrastructure to fully automate deliveries and eliminate human driving jobs altogether.

title: McDonald’s and Walmart Are Part of the Widening Fray Over Surveillance Pricing
snippet: The Federal Trade Commission has urged companies to be transparent about their pricing, but that may not be enough.
fullText:
The debate over whether companies can set prices based on information they have about individual customers continues to grow. So-called surveillance pricing is in the news again on reports that Walmart patented technology for dynamic AI pricing about six months after filing for patents related to digital shelf labels.

Walmart, faced with a backlash, has been trying to assure the public that different customers will see the same digital shelf label prices and that its backend AI systems won’t engage in discriminatory pricing. “Your income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay won’t change the price,” Walmart CEO John Furner wrote in a Sept. 25 letter to customers. “And whether you’re buying groceries or electronics on a hot afternoon or in a sudden rush for an item, it’s never a reason to charge you more.”

Reached for comment, a representative for Walmart pointed CNET to the web page and letter to customers regarding pricing.

			

More from CNET

“Walmart does not set different prices based on who you are or the time of day, and we won’t,” the representative said in an email. “A patent does not define Walmart’s pricing practices or intent.”

But the backlash may continue if customers aren’t convinced. One consumer advocate, Jeff Rossen, went as far as to suggest in a recent video that Walmart customers should leave their phones in the car when they shop in order to avoid being datamined. 

Separately, but in a similar vein, McDonald’s has been the target of media coverage over its shift to AI systems that could mean different prices for different burgers at different restaurants for different customers. The company has bristled at some of that coverage, calling it “speculative and misinformed,” but it hasn’t stopped reporters from asking why burger prices can vary from neighborhood to neighborhood as part of the company’s technology makeover.

A representative for McDonald’s didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Two of the largest American brands are now caught in the publicity crossfire over a topic that is drawing attention from lawmakers, the Federal Trade Commission and consumer advocacy groups: how companies are using AI to set prices and whether those practices may harm certain shoppers or even break the law.

Surveillance pricing, which is often conflated with the terms “dynamic pricing” or “algorithmic pricing,” is a broad term that includes something that’s been happening for decades: prices set automatically based on supply and demand (say, gasoline prices). For years, shoppers also heard about “surge pricing,” such as the cost of an Uber ride increasingly dramatically during spikes in activity or around big events.

But as AI has gone mainstream and more companies have access to an array of information collected about their customers — whether it’s through apps, loyalty programs or just website tracking — it’s increasingly likely that those companies can set different prices for different shoppers based on that information.

It may not always be personal: In June, a lawsuit was filed in California claiming gas stations were inflating the price of fuel illegally due to AI software used by thousands of gas stations. But lawmakers in states are concerned about more personalized dynamic pricing. This summer, New Jersey passed a law set to go into effect in 2027 banning the use of personal data to set prices; the law primarily targets grocery stores.

Walmart’s new digital shelf labels, like these seen in Albany, New York, can update prices automatically. Consumers are worried that means prices can change unexpectedly based on who’s shopping.Larry Rulison/Albany Times Union/Getty Images

Last year, shoppers in New York began seeing warnings on product pages due to new laws mandating that customers let people know when shopping prices were set using personal data in an algorithm. 

According to the Electronic Privacy Information Center, for instance, personal data and market data are being used by retailers to determine the highest price a customer is willing to pay, leading to higher prices.

In a report released in August, the Consumer Federation of America called out retailers, hotel booking sites and airlines for engaging in practices like raising prices based on things like how much AI determined they’d be willing to pay, their income or their proximity to a store.

What the FTC is doing

The Federal Trade Commission said in August that it’s looking for public comment on policy around surveillance pricing, but it has implied that it may not be able to do much to stop companies by enforcing rules; its approach appears to be geared toward helping consumers be more aware of potential surveillance pricing and requesting that those engaging in this kind of pricing be transparent about it.

That’s not enough, according to consumer advocates like the CFA, which responded to the FTC’s proposal with a letter demanding it do more than promote transparency.

“Not even the most detailed disclosure of what information they’re using to hike your prices will change the fact that those prices are still going up,” said Emily Peterson-Cassin, director of competition and market fairness at the CFA, told CNET in an email. The CFA argues in its letter that surveillance prices can be based on proxies for protected characteristics like race or age and are likely to disproportionately hurt low-income and working families who can’t easily comparison shop.

“To put it bluntly, the more vulnerable you are, the harder you stand to get hit,” Peterson-Cassin said. “If companies know you must have, for example, baby formula, they are more likely to charge you a higher price for it. “

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Omar Gallaga
						

						

											

								

											Omar Gallaga has covered technology, digital culture and other topics for outlets including CNET, NPR, WIRED, Texas Monthly, MSNBC, Consumer Reports, The Washington Post, the Los Angeles Times, The Atlantic and the Austin American-Statesman, where he was a longtime tech reporter, editor and podcaster. He lives in the Texas Hill Country.

title: Samsung Suddenly Raises Prices by $100 on Most Galaxy S26 Phones
snippet: An S26 Ultra with 1TB of storage now lists for $2,000.
fullText:
Call it what you want: RAMageddon, chipflation, the AI tax. Amid a global memory shortage that’s compelling companies to hike prices on phones, PCs, laptops and gaming consoles, our devices keep getting more expensive. 

On Thursday, Samsung quietly raised prices on the Galaxy S26, S26 Plus and S26 Ultra by $100, without issuing an official company statement. The Galaxy S26 FE didn’t go up in price, and Samsung’s newest foldables — Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra and Z Flip 8 — were also spared the carnage.

For the larger 512GB models, the Galaxy S26 now lists at $1,200, the S26 Plus at $1,400, and the S26 Ultra at $1,600. The S26 Ultra with 1TB storage went up $200 and is now $2,000. All the company’s smartphone prices are listed here.

		

			

A Samsung representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The RAM shortage is a result of the massive buildout of AI data center infrastructure, which requires huge amounts of memory, especially high-bandwidth memory, or HBM. Apple and Google also raised prices by about $100 on their most recent phones.

Read more: Why RAMageddon Might Force Apps and Operating Systems’ Performance to Suck Less

Is there relief in sight?

In its Q2 earnings call in July, Samsung said it expects the memory shortage to be worse next year and persist through 2028.

At Amazon, the S26 Ultra is still available at lower prices. It’s not yet known whether any of the Galaxy S26 phones will be available during October Prime Day, Oct. 6 and 7, but check out CNET’s constantly updated coverage of all the deals.

Cellphone carriers such as Verizon, T-Mobile and AT&T could mitigate some sticker shock with installment plans, trade-in credits and refurbished devices. But that won’t reverse higher prices nor solve the memory shortage problem, GlobalData senior analyst Amanda Mitchell said in a new analysis.

“Lasting relief depends on additional production capacity, but manufacturers’ expansion plans will take years to reach the market, and much of the new investment is intended to serve AI demand rather than consumer devices,” Mitchell said. “With meaningful new capacity years away, price pressure is likely to persist.”

Update, September 30, 7:37 p.m. ET: Apple says all of the outages have now been resolved, with the exception of Apple TV.

Update, October 1, 8:00 p.m. ET: Apple says the Apple TV issue has finally been resolved.

Apple is currently reporting issues affecting Apple TV and subscription purchases, while some users are also running into problems elsewhere across the company’s services. Here are the details.

Apple currently lists 8 active issues

Apple’s System Status page currently lists Apple TV, App Store, Apple Fitness+, Apple Music, Apple Music Subscriptions, Mac App Store, and Subscription Purchase as experiencing outages or other ongoing issues.

According to Apple, most of the issues began at 4:22 p.m. ET. The company lists the App Store, Apple Music, and Mac App Store as undergoing “routine maintenance, with no expected user impact,” while the Apple TV outage began at 4:43 p.m. ET, with Apple warning that the service “may be unavailable due to scheduled maintenance.”

In our testing, the Apple TV interface failed to load on iOS, although content continued to load and play normally on other devices.

	

The outages began shortly after apps, including TestFlight, the App Store, and Fitness+, started displaying internal localization strings in place of normal interface text. It is unclear whether that is related to the other issues Apple’s systems are currently facing.

Reports on Downdetector further confirm the issue affecting Apple TV, though they appear to have already peaked and are now trending down, suggesting the outage may be gradually subsiding.

We will monitor the situation and update this post once more information becomes available, or Apple marks the issues as resolved.

title: Here’s how much Google is testing paying web publishers for AI Overview usage
snippet: A new report details how Google is testing paying web publishers for content used in its AI Overviews, including how much they’re making and how much that varies. more…
fullText:
A new report details how Google is testing paying web publishers for content used in its AI Overviews, including how much they’re making and how much that varies.

Google’s AI Overviews have drastically reshaped the web, and it’s hard to argue that it hasn’t harmed publishers across the web. Traffic is down almost universally, though Google insists AI isn’t to blame. Still, Google’s AI Overviews and other AI responses rely on publishers around the web to continue operating, something that’s increasingly difficult to do.

Following a report earlier this month, The Information is now offering a few more details on Google’s test to directly pay web publishers when their content is used in AI Overviews. 

The company is apparently paying around 100 digital publishers including “small to midsize blogs and websites.” Revenue seems to vary wildly, though. For some, it amounts to “less than one-tenth of 1% of their advertising revenue.” Some “smaller sites” have apparently earned less than $1,000 over several months, where another publisher that “joined a few months ago” has already made around $50,000-60,000 so far, “which doesn’t represent that much of its business.” Yet, another publisher said that a “bigger slice” was covered with Google’s payments earning “more than $1 million a year.”

	

The test, as previously reported, gives publishers insights into how often AI Overviews leverage their content. What’s not yet clear is how Google determines how much a publisher is paid, with some finding that “less widely covered” topics that “draw strong user interest” currently earn more, with examples including anime and gaming. 

It’s still unclear if Google plans to expand this program, but The Information reiterates that Google “needs these web publishers to stay active” for its models and answers to stay current and accurate.

title: Google announces Gemini 4 Argon as its new frontier model
snippet: Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s “next era of frontier intelligence” and built for “deep reasoning across complex, long-horizon workflows.” It follows the cancellation of Gemini 3.5 Pro and focus on 3.8 Flash. more…
fullText:
Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s “next era of frontier intelligence” and built for “deep reasoning across complex, long-horizon workflows.” It follows the cancellation of Gemini 3.5 Pro and focus on 3.8 Flash.

With this new model (which has a new naming scheme), Google wants to offer “frontier-level capabilities” across coding, knowledge work, cybersecurity defense, and creative writing.

Gemini 4 Argon’s output token limit is 1M tokens (up from 64K) to allow for longer and more complex use cases. This is paired with expanded coding, reasoning, and multimodal capabilities.

When the model has the headroom to think deeply and generate hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single trajectory, it adds a new level of depth in reasoning to solve tough problems in one go.

In terms of benchmarks, Google touts a DeepSWE v1.1 score of 77.9%. Claude Opus 5.5 comes in at 74.2% followed by GPT-6 Astra’s 74.1%.

	

Google trained Gemini 4 Argon to be “highly capable at cybersecurity defense” with leaps over 3.8 Flash Cyber. The model will be made available “without cyber guardrails” to trusted defenders and internal Google teams so that they can “leverage its full frontier-level cybersecurity defense capabilities.”

“On CWE-bench v1, which evaluates the model’s ability to remediate security vulnerabilities, Argon ties for first place with a top score of 68%”

Outside of coding, Gemini 4 Argon also has “leading performance across other domain specific evaluations,” such as Vals Finance Agent v2 (multi-step financial research) and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (legal research and drafting).

“On AutomationBench, Zapier’s benchmark measuring end-to-end execution across core business functions, Argon ranks #1 with a score of 51.3%.”

“…on LVBench, which measures long video understanding, Argon is state of the art with a score of 91.7%.”

Gemini 4 Argon is “rolling out soon,” starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers and paid API customers. 

“Argon will launch at an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.”

“After the introductory period expires, the price of $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens will apply.”

So far, it has been made available to trusted testers and cyber defenders (via Fairwind Program). Before the broader release, Google is focusing on:

Defending against misuse from cyber or chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) attacks: Google has improved “techniques to monitor the model’s internal activations to spot misuse.”

Defending against prompt injection attacks: Google’s “most resilient model yet against indirect prompt injections” with “leading in prompt injection robustness on the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark.”

Hardening systems: “we are hardening our sandboxed environments by isolating and sealing them before high-risk training or evaluations begin.”

Monitoring for misalignment: Google is “deploying misalignment mitigations that monitor Argon’s chain-of-thought and actions and stop execution when necessary.”

“We used a similar system to monitor our training runs and send alerts to a dedicated incident response team, taking careful precautions against feeding the findings back into training so as to not risk shaping Argon’s reasoning to evade our monitoring.”

Inside Google, Gemini 4 Argon is already powering internal workflows with “thousands of Googlers highlighting the model’s strengths in specialized coding tasks, conducting deeper research, and writing quality.” The company shared some examples today:

Memory efficiency: A team of Argon agents analyzed fleet-wide profiling telemetry to autonomously identify and apply memory optimizations across Google’s data centers, freeing up over 300 TiB of memory once rolled out, with an estimated 500 TiB to 1 PiB in total savings.

Large Scale Codebase Migrations and Optimizations: Argon agents are working on migrating C/C++ codebases to Rust across Google—scaling from tens of thousands of lines in core libraries like re2, libgav1 up to 800K+ lines for the Fuchsia OS Zircon kernel. Given the criticality of many of these systems, such large-scale rewrites are undergoing rigorous automated and manual auditing, emulation testing, and review before rolling out to production.

For libgav1, Google’s open source software for decoding video, Argon agents took an existing Rust port and replaced 32K lines of SIMD code by running many rounds of profile-guided experiments, studying the compiler’s output, producing safe Rust so the compiler would vectorize it automatically. The end result is a memory-safe video decoder that runs 2.7x faster than the Rust port, with identical video output, bringing it closer to the optimized C++.

fullText:

title: Apple’s HomePad smart home hub launching on Oct 13 with iMac G4 design – Bloomberg
snippet: Apple’s long-awaited smart home hub, which we’ve been referring to as the HomePad, is set to launch on October 13, according to Bloomberg. The device is said to feature a 6-inch display and a design inspired by the iMac G4, and will launch alongside a HomePod mini update with new colors and a new Apple TV 4K with Siri AI support … more…
fullText:
Apple’s long-awaited smart home hub, which we’ve been referring to as the HomePad, is set to launch on October 13, according to Bloomberg.

The device is said to feature a 6-inch display and a design inspired by the iMac G4, and will launch alongside a HomePod mini update with new colors and a new Apple TV 4K with Siri AI support …

A previous report from the same source had said only that it was expected to launch “as soon as October,” but the latest report specifies October 13th.

Apple Inc. plans to make its long-delayed push into the smart-home market on Oct. 13, marking a critical product expansion for the company under new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus.

The iMac G4 was one of the company’s most iconic designs, with a hemispherical base and a free-floating screen that could be rotated, raised, lowered, and tilted to position it anywhere you wanted. I said a year ago that I very much hoped Apple would bring back this beautiful design for the upcoming product.

It’s previously been reported that the device will come in two versions: the tabletop one referenced here, and a second version intended to be mounted on a wall.

	

The upcoming device is expected to include a speaker to enable it to act as a HomePod as well as a smart home control panel. It’s expected to have a new operating system combining elements of iOS, tvOS, and watchOS – and to center around Siri AI.

Daring Fireball separately suggested that iPhone Duo review models would be handed over to tech writers on October 13 or 14, and that as Apple likes to do this in-person for high-profile products it would make sense to combine this with an event for the new products.

Today’s report says that the device is codenamed J490. Do you expect to buy one? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Pages, Keynote, Numbers, and Pixelmator Pro just got new features
snippet: Today alongside a big update to Final Cut Camera, Apple announced that it’s rolling out updated versions of Pages, Keynote, Numbers, Pixelmator Pro, and Freeform. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Today alongside a big update to Final Cut Camera, Apple announced that it’s rolling out updated versions of Pages, Keynote, Numbers, Pixelmator Pro, and Freeform. Here’s what’s new.

Apple rolling out updates to ‘Creator Studio’ apps, but non-subscribers get new features too

Apple has announced new features coming to its popular iWork suite today—Pages, Keynote, and Numbers—alongside improvements for Pixelmator Pro and Freeform.

Some additions are exclusive to Apple Creator Studio, but select features will be available for all users. Here’s everything new, per Apple Newsroom:

Pages, Keynote, Numbers

Apple says that today’s updates bring support for asking Siri questions about Pages, Keynote, or Numbers and get answers. It’s unclear if Siri AI is required or not, but that’s likely. The updates also enable “the ability to request access to a shared presentation, document, or spreadsheet.” This makes collaboration easier, as the file owner no longer needs to initiate file sharing.

Pages for Mac has a new Screen View, which “optimizes content for reading and focused writing.” And Numbers gets “new trigonometry, statistics, and logic functions for solving complex problems in a spreadsheet.”

Additionally, for Apple Creator Studio subscribers there are new templates and themes available across all three iWork apps. And in Keynote, intelligent slide generation will automatically make images that are tailored to a given presentation.

Pixelmator Pro

Pixelmator Pro on iPad adds Select and Mask tools that were previously Mac-exclusive. And both Mac and iPad apps gain two template collections for sports and action-centric projects, plus new templates for “launching a new creative idea, business, or product.”

	

Additionally, there’s a new Podcasts category for creating cover artwork that’s sized to fit well on major podcast platforms.

Freeform

Freeform gains several highly requested features. Boards now automatically adapt to Dark Mode, and folders let users organize boards into collections and invite others to collaborate. Writing Tools with Apple Intelligence can rewrite, proofread, and summarize handwritten notes; users can also request access to collaborate on shared files, or automate adding content using Shortcuts. Freeform becomes even more powerful in visionOS 27, letting users pull multiple items from a board — including images, videos, sticky notes, shapes, and 3D models — into their space, and view 3D models together as a group.

title: Tesla sustains its EV sales momentum despite US troubles
snippet: The company delivered more than 486,000 EVs in the third quarter, down from last year's record but moving in a positive direction.
fullText:
Tesla sold more than 480,000 EVs in the third quarter, as the company continues finding ways to move new cars despite its troubles in the U.S. market. 

It was the second strong quarter in a row for Tesla after a somewhat rough start to the year. The sales figure easily beat out consensus estimates from Wall Street and topped even the most optimistic view for the company, which made its 10 millionth vehicle earlier this year. 

The company said Friday morning that it built 464,391 vehicles in the quarter and delivered more than 486,532. That’s an increase of roughly 6,000 vehicle deliveries compared to the second quarter. But sales were still down from the same period last year, when Tesla delivered 497,000 vehicles. That quarter — Tesla’s best ever — was helped by a rush of U.S. buyers who were looking to take advantage of an expiring federal tax credit.

Before Friday’s numbers were released, Tesla’s sales were down nearly 20% year-over-year in the U.S. market, according to Cox Automotive.

That drop has been the result of a number of factors. Tesla has not released any new consumer models in years — with the exception of the Cybertruck, which has been a commercial flop. Potential buyers have also balked because of Elon Musk’s personal support of Donald Trump’s presidential campaign and his role overseeing the Department of Government Efficiency, which laid off thousands of workers and canceled international aid funding.

Tesla has looked to other markets to make up for lost U.S. sales. The company’s sales are on the rise again in Europe, where EVs are more widely adopted and supported by tighter emissions regulations. Tesla is reportedly expanding capacity at its factory in Germany to meet that demand. The company has also seen continued strong sales out of its factory in China despite competition in the region, with some of those sales driven by Tesla looking to newer markets like Japan, Australia, and Lithuania.

Despite the rebound in overall momentum, sales have become something of a taboo subject for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who is increasingly focused on the company’s other efforts. Perhaps the biggest example is the Cybercab, which Tesla started putting on the roads of Austin, Texas in recent weeks. The two-seater EV has been giving autonomous rides to passengers despite having no driver, steering wheel, or pedals.

Tesla also recently launched the production version of its electric big rig, nearly a decade after it was first introduced. The company aims to make roughly 50,000 Tesla Semi vehicles per year.

Other new efforts are in the works, but don’t have firm commercial timelines. The second-generation Roadster is set to be re-revealed on October 15 after years of delays, though it’s not clear when it will get built. Tesla is also developing the Optimus humanoid robot, but has repeatedly pushed back its timeline. Earlier this week, Tesla announced it had secured up to $30 billion in new lines of credit to support these projects.

When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

		

Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane.

title: The Pocket Advance nearly perfects my favorite Nintendo handheld
snippet: Although I count the original Game Boy as one of my first tech obsessions, I still consider Nintendo’s Game Boy Advance to be my favorite console of all time thanks to its more comfortable horizontal design (for my big hands) and its expansive catalog of excellent 32-bit and 16-bit games. Ayaneo isn’t the first company to attempt to modernize the GBA, but its Konkr Pocket Advance does it best. The handheld strikes a near perfect balance between authentically re-creating the GBA’s design while updating its hardware with new controls, a much better screen, and the flexibility of Android at a price that feels like a bargain. As much as I still adore the GBA, I’ve eagerly embraced upgrades to the aging console over the years. First it was the clamshell GBA SP that finally delivered a frontlit screen I could actually see without a lamp over my shoulder, and later it was aftermarket upgrades like a backlit LCD display and a rechargeable battery that vastly improved Nintendo’s original hardware. Two years ago, I eagerly purchased Anbernic’s GBA-inspired RG34XX, but all of those have now been replaced by the Konkr Pocket Advance. It’s my first handheld from Ayaneo, and I’ve been pleasantly surprised to find the hardware feels on par with Nintendo’s. The Pocket Advance is an all-plastic affair but with a satisfying heft thanks to extra internal hardware including a cooling fan for its MediaTek Helio G90T processor and a 4,000mAh battery. I opted for the cheaper $109 version with 3GB of RAM and 32GB of storage, which is expandable with a microSD card, but for $129, you can get 4GB of RAM with 64GB of storage built-in. It’s not an exact copy of the GBA, but the Pocket Advance’s dimensions are close enough to fit all the cases I’ve somehow preserved for the past 25 years. Where Ayaneo’s remake really diverges from the original is with eight additional buttons including X and Y action buttons plus four extra shoulder buttons on the top edge. I’m a big fan of the larger D-pad Ayaneo has included, but some retro gaming purists may not be fans of how soft and squishy the Pocket Advance’s buttons all feel. I’ve had to learn to mash the action buttons just a little harder to ensure presses are always registered, but I don’t necessarily think the button feel is a downside because they’re also satisfyingly quiet. The Pocket Advance’s 3.5-inch LCD touchscreen with a glass cover is an excellent upgrade, but it does cater to GBA games with a 3:2 aspect ratio and a 960×640 resolution allowing them to be perfectly scaled at 4x. (The GBA had a 240×160 screen resolution.) Unless you’re a monster who can tolerate playing games that have been stretched vertically or horizontally to fill a screen, emulating games from other systems will result in letterboxing or pillarboxing on the sides, and potentially some visual artifacts from scaling when the math isn’t perfect. Most similarly sized and similarly priced handhelds run some variation of Linux. There’s a thriving community of developers creating and porting a large assortment of emulators, games, and apps to Linux, but installing, configuring, customizing and updating software is not always a user-friendly process, especially for novices who may only be familiar with using plug-and-play game carts. The Pocket Advance instead comes with Android 12, and while that version feels a little dated, setting up the handheld will feel a little more familiar to anyone with smartphone experience. Ayaneo Konkr Pocket Advance An authentic but upgraded clone of Nintendo’s Game Boy Advance that can play more than just GBA games using emulation. Where to Buy: $109 at Ayaneo Getting the Pocket Advance up and running was relatively easy thanks in part to Ayaneo’s custom launcher called AYASpace that makes it easier to install various emulators. But the handheld also has access to the Google Play Store, or you can install Android apps or add-ons downloaded directly from a website. I’m a big fan of a clean and simple launcher for Linux handhelds called MinUI, so instead of AYASpace, I installed an alternative Android launcher called Cannoli on the Pocket Advance that brings the same aesthetics with several emulators preinstalled and preconfigured. The flexibility of Android means I can set the Pocket Advance to load Cannoli by default, but I have the option to switch back to AYASpace at any time, or install and jump between multiple alternatives. When it comes to emulation capabilities, you’ll want to keep your expectations limited to “retro” gaming. The Pocket Advance’s seven-year-old processor is powerful enough to handle many titles from the PS2 and GameCube, but the handheld is better equipped to emulate the PS1 and Sega Dreamcast, and you’ll have the best experience with games from even older consoles like the Super Nintendo and Genesis. An easy-access quick settings menu that slides in from the right lets you quickly customize and reconfigure the handheld including boosting its performance (at the cost of battery life) to handle more intensive games, but another thing preventing the Pocket Advance from playing more modern games is its lack of analog thumbsticks. Performance and compatibility will also vary with native Android games and apps. I’ve had a lot of fun playing through Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder’s Revenge once again, but while the Pocket Advance is a passable way to stream Netflix, I can’t get it to play any Disney Plus content without the app crashing out. Anbernic’s $69.99 RG34XX is still cheaper than the Pocket Advance and may seem like a better alternative, but I think Ayaneo’s is absolutely worth the extra $40. It’s a more powerful and capable handheld with a higher-res display, and I much prefer the Pocket Advance’s larger D-pad and shoulder button arrangement. I also find the quality of Anbernic’s hardware to be hit and miss. Similar to what others have reported on Reddit, I’ve experienced intermittent issues with the responsiveness of the RG34XX’s D-pad. I haven’t had the motivation to crack it open to attempt a DIY fix, and with the Pocket Advance now in my collection, it’s doubtful I ever will. The Pocket Advance is one of the best retro handhelds currently available and not just because of its nostalgic retro design. As long as you temper your gaming expectations and won’t be frustrated by what it can’t play, it’s an excellent way to revisit and enjoy games from Nintendo’s earlier handheld era. The Pocket Advance (left) with its larger screen and extra controls next to an upgraded original Game Boy Advance (right).

The D-pad on the Pocket Advance (right) is larger than what the original GBA (left) featured and feels better under my larger thumb.

The Pocket Advance’s 3.5-inch LCD touchscreen with a glass cover is an excellent upgrade, but it does cater to GBA games with a 3:2 aspect ratio and a 960x640 resolution allowing them to be perfectly scaled at 4x. The Pocket Advance includes a headphone jack and features a small dial for adjusting volume instead of buttons.

Most similarly sized and similarly priced handhelds run some variation of Linux. There’s a thriving community of developers creating and porting a large assortment of emulators, games, and apps to Linux, but installing, configuring, customizing and updating software is not always a user-friendly process, especially for novices who may only be familiar with using plug-and-play game carts. The Pocket Advance instead comes with Android 12, and while that version feels a little dated, setting up the handheld will feel a little more familiar to anyone with smartphone experience.

An authentic but upgraded clone of Nintendo’s Game Boy Advance that can play more than just GBA games using emulation.

On the top edge of the Pocket Advance, you’ll find three pairs of shoulder buttons alongside a power button and an additional one that’s customizable.

Performance and compatibility will also vary with native Android games and apps. The Pocket Advance (bottom) is similar to Anbernic’s RG34XX (top,) but feels like a higher quality handheld overall.
