title: M6 Mac release schedule: Here’s when to expect new Macs
snippet: Apple next-generation M6 chip arrived last week in the new Mac mini. But several more products will get M6 upgrades soon. Here’s the rumored release schedule for M6 Macs—plus the M6 iPad Pro. more…
fullText:
Apple next-generation M6 chip arrived last week in the new Mac mini. But several more products will get M6 upgrades soon. Here’s the rumored release schedule for M6 Macs—plus the M6 iPad Pro.

This fall: M6 MacBook Pro, M6 iMac

This fall, likely in October or early November, Apple is rumored to launch two new M6 Macs:

MacBook Pro

iMac

The MacBook Pro will be only the 14-inch base model. Per Mark Gurman, Apple is skipping Pro and Max versions of the M6 chip. As a result, only the entry MacBook Pro will get M6 while the next Pro-level chips coming will be M7 Pro and M7 Max in 2027.

Apple’s new iMac isn’t expected to change much beyond the M6 chip. The only other rumored upgrade is a fresh slate of colors. But the jump from M4 to M6 should make the new model a worthy update nonetheless.

Notably absent from this list is the rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro / Ultra. It’s expected to launch soon too, but will use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips instead of the M6.

Early 2027: M6 MacBook Air, M6 iPad Pro

After this fall, the next products rumored to get M6 upgrades are:

MacBook Air

iPad Pro

A new M6 MacBook Air is expected to launch in early 2027. Anytime in the February-April window is possible, but based on Apple’s history, March is a safe bet.

Other than a chip upgrade, there are minimal rumors about the new MacBook Air. It should retain the same design as the M5 model. And reporting dates an OLED upgrade as coming no sooner than 2028, so the display will likely be unchanged too.

Apple last updated the iPad Pro in fall 2025, when it got the M5 chip. Rumors point to a spring 2027 update coming, meaning the product will follow its typical 18-month upgrade cycle.

Beyond getting the M6 chip, Apple’s new iPad Pro is expected to add a vapor chamber for cooling. That should boost sustained performance in the ultra-thin device.

One potential M6 benefit for both the MacBook Air and iPad Pro is that it could boost battery life. Apple says the M6’s 2-nanometer process brings “a major leap in performance and power efficiency.”

Around the same time, Apple TV subscribers also got the return of Slow Horses, alongside recent releases including the Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh-led Mayday and the much-anticipated fourth season of Ted Lasso.

According to Deadline, this perfect storm helped Apple TV record its “highest weekly viewership ever for the week of Sept. 14, rising by +67% year-over-year.”

From Deadline:

Released straight-to-streaming on Sept. 4, Mayday has become Apple TV’s biggest film debut on the platform to date over its first 18 days, the company said. In the U.S., Mayday opened at No. 1 in Luminate’s Sept. 4-10 weekly rankings with 8.7M views. It remained strong in Week 2, placing at No.2.

The site also notes that, according to Apple TV, Widow’s Bay saw a whopping 280% week-over-week increase in viewership during the week after the Emmys, where it took home 14 awards, including Outstanding Comedy Series.

Apple TV noted that the increase was particularly notable in “the US, UK, Canada, Australia, Brazil, Mexico, Germany, India, Poland, and Spain,” says Deadline.

The company added that Pluribus saw a similar effect following its six Emmy wins, including Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series for Rhea Seehorn. The series “experienced a 200% surge in viewership week-over-week following the ceremony,” according to Apple.

Finally, Deadline notes that while the Emmys and recent premieres certainly helped drive the gains, Apple’s recent iCloud+ expansion may also have played a role.

Earlier this month, Apple began including Apple TV with iCloud+ at no extra charge in more than 100 countries, a rollout that also brought the streaming service to 59 new markets for the first time, expanding its total reach to 170 countries.

title: This startup wants to turn idle car inventory into rental revenue
snippet: When Igor Dobrianskyi looks at a car dealership lot, he doesn't see rows of cars — he sees millions of dollars just sitting there, depreciating. Come see MyMonthlyCar in the Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13 to 15 in San Francisco.
fullText:
When Igor Dobrianskyi looks at a car dealership lot, he sees a wasted opportunity. 

“Millions and millions of used cars are sitting on parking lots, depreciating and losing value,” Dobrianskyi said in a recent interview, adding that there are 76,000 dealerships in the United States. “At the same time, there are people who need a car for a few months, but the options are actually very limited and expensive.”

Dobrianskyi’s new startup, MyMonthlyCar, aims to connect both sides of that equation through an online platform that offers flexible month-to-month rentals from local dealerships. MyMonthlyCar was selected for the 2026 Startup Battlefield 200, a cohort of promising early-stage startups that have earned a spot to exhibit at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13 to 15 in San Francisco.

MyMonthlyCar, which is registered in Delaware and based in Florida, was co-founded by Dobrianskyi; CPO Kostiantyn Gitko; and CTO Vadym Zotov. All three are from Ukraine, said Dobrianskyi, who moved to the U.S. with his wife and young daughter after the Russia-Ukraine war began.

MyMonthlyCar does what its name suggests, with one twist: The startup only rents used cars on a month-to-month basis; no short-term options here. But it does give dealerships the chance to offer customers a rent-to-own option.

“So we don’t bring them only customers to rent on a monthly basis; we basically bring them the clients who potentially can buy this car as well,” he said.

MyMonthlyCar doesn’t charge dealerships to list cars on its website. Instead, MyMonthlyCar charges dealers 10% of each transaction. It also charges the customer a separate 10% fee.

The idea for MyMonthlyCar stems from Dobrianskyi’s previous experience in the industry. The founder owned a car rental company in Ukraine, but the lack of financing options there limited his ability to scale. In 2016, he launched a peer-to-peer car marketplace called SizeCar, where owners rent their cars to other drivers, much like Turo does today. SizeCar eventually spread to 40 European cities.

The startup has signed on seven dealerships to test the service and is working with an insurance broker to finalize its own insurance program, which will let customers choose among different types of coverage.

“Insurance is the key for this business, and you need to have your own insurance as a platform,” he said, noting that the No. 1 question from dealers was about insurance and liability coverage. 

Despite its early-stage status, the founders have bullish projections for the startup. They plan to sign on 100 dealerships with 2,000 monthly rentals and $300,000 in revenue in the company’s first year of operation, which will kick off later this year once the insurance program launches. Over the next five years, the goal is to generate $42 million in revenue, Dobrianskyi said.

The startup has yet to raise venture capital and is currently bootstrapped. But Dobrianskyi said the plan is to raise a seed round, with the funds helping the company hire more developers to build out the platform, including an AI tool to help dealers identify which cars are best to rent out at any given time. 

To check out MyMonthlyCar and the other startups that are part of TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield competition (as well as to network with the folks funding them), join us next month at Disrupt.

This week saw the debut of Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon chips and, with it, the usual onslaught of Tensor hate around Google’s Pixel phones. Personally, I don’t care about those, but new launches around Qualcomm’s event have shown off a lot of other specs I’d much rather see Pixel adopt.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

Google’s Tensor chip in Pixel phones has been a hot-button issue for enthusiasts for the entire time Google has been working on the project. And, I get it. Tensor is objectively not as powerful as a flagship Snapdragon or MediaTek chip and, with Pixel phones getting more and more expensive, that’s hard to accept. Google has solved many of the biggest deficiencies, leading to fairly wide acceptance from the “average Joe” customer base that Google is aiming for in the first place, but every year the same conversation comes back up with a new Snapdragon chip – “I wish that was in my Pixel.”

Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 family – I’m choosing to not put “Extreme” into that word salad here – looks incredible, and MediaTek’s new Dimensity 9600 Pro is also going to be solid. It’s totally okay to be annoyed that Pixels don’t get the same raw horsepower.

	

But, for me at least, it’s everything else that I wish Google would get a bit more on board with.

This week’s new chip launches also saw the announcement of new phones using those chips and, man, it’s wild how much faster these other brands are progressing compared to market staples like Pixel and Galaxy. The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Oppo Find X10 look insane. 

Xiaomi 18 Pro series goes official with ‘privacy screen,’ 8,500 mAh battery, and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

Oppo Find X10 series goes official with triple 200MP cameras, 8,000 mAh battery

8,000+ mAh batteries, a plethora of 200MP cameras, that’s the sort of stuff I wish I was getting on my Pixel. Forget horsepower, give me battery life and camera sensors that look good even before the power of computational photography steps in. The Oppo Find X9 Ultra was a big wake-up for me in that regard, as it was the first phone in quite a while that made me want to ditch the Pixel from my phone lineup (and I’m sure our Inbox author Daniel Bader is greatly enjoying it after prying it from my “Techtember”-ed fingers).

Google, if you’re listening, the rest of the Android world is frankly killing it on the hardware front right now. The software is still so-so in my book, but the practical wins that come from these all-out builds are too great to ignore. So, Pixel 12 maybe? Thanks.

title: AI hallucinations are making entitled customers even worse
snippet: Madison, a server in New York City, greets every table by asking about each diner's allergies. Lately, there have been some close calls. fullText:
Madison, a server in New York City, greets every table by asking about each diner’s allergies. Lately, there have been some close calls. “Sometimes people will tell me they have a shellfish allergy, and I’ll come back, and they won’t ask me any questions,” says Madison, who asked that her last name be withheld to protect her identity. “And they’ll order a fish dish that comes with a broth that is made of shellfish.”

When she tells them a dish contains an allergen, she’s had guests push back, saying ChatGPT disagrees. “They just want to talk to ChatGPT,” Madison explains. “You’re allergic to shellfish, and ChatGPT says there’s no shellfish in this, and we are telling you, yes there is!”

Mass adoption of generative AI tools is rewriting the old adage that has long been a thorn in the side of restaurant and retail workers: “The customer is always right.” But what happens when the customer expects you to play along with something AI made up?

Beyond ignoring her warnings about allergens, Madison has noticed an increased reliance on generative AI among patrons at the Michelin-recommended Italian restaurant where she worked until recently. “The amount of times I’ve suggested, ‘Let me grab the sommelier for you,’ and they say, ‘No, I’ll just ask ChatGPT,’ or somms have been dismissed from the table because the guest has a preference for ChatGPT, that has been increasing quite a bit,” she says. She’s had customers request bottles that the restaurant doesn’t carry — or, in some cases, that don’t exist at all.

For Madison, these AI hallucinations exacerbate some people’s preexisting anxieties about wine. “Some people have always had an issue with sommeliers, thinking ‘These people are like used car salesmen trying to get us to spend way more than we want to on a bottle of wine,’” she says, “or there are people who get in their heads and think, ‘The sommelier is going to think I’m stupid.’” To “soften the blow” of AI hallucinations, Madison and her colleagues will say things like, “We have this really hyper-specific wine list, maybe it’s showing you a French wine, and we don’t carry French wine,” instead of telling the customer their AI chatbot completely made up a wine brand.

You’re allergic to shellfish, and ChatGPT says there’s no shellfish in this, and we are telling you, yes there is!

The AI creep is seemingly ubiquitous in customer service jobs now. The launch of Muse, Meta’s new AI agent, will likely exacerbate the issue — and the headaches for workers who have to field customers’ occasionally nonsensical requests. In reporting this story, I heard from movie theater workers, baristas, and Apple Store employees, all of whom have had customers ask for products or features that don’t exist. On Reddit and X, customer service workers are complaining about customers who take ChatGPT’s word as gospel.

Jason, a river ranger who works on federal lands in the Mountain West, says he’s noticed an increase in visitors arriving to the park with nonsensical AI-generated itineraries.

“My colleagues and I have explained that the AI hallucinated campsites or scheduled things out of geographical order, so the group would have to row their boats upstream some days (not possible) and float with the river current other days,” says Jason, who asked to be referred to by a pseudonym because he’s a federal employee. “The craziest part is that even with a ranger explaining this while pointing at a map, we’ve had multiple groups remain skeptical. A certain type of AI user is inclined to trust ChatGPT over rangers, maps, and printed guidebooks.”

Casey, an after-school program teacher in New York who asked to be referred to by a pseudonym, says she’s noticed many students’ parents, nannies, and other caretakers are now turning to ChatGPT or Claude for their questions on childhood development.

“We had one family that consulted ChatGPT to come up with a bedtime routine and sleep schedule for their kid, but their kid wasn’t getting quite enough sleep,” Casey says. Based on his behavior in the program, Casey estimated that the child needed two to three more hours of sleep a night, and told his parents this. “The parents just insisted that their ChatGPT was telling them that their schedule was fine.”

Some parents, she says, now see generative AI tools as experts whose knowledge surpasses that of childcare professionals. “It can be really hard to talk with somebody who has made their mind up,” Casey says, “because they trust this outside entity as being invaluable.” She’s also noticed more anodyne uses of the technology, like kids coming in with AI-generated coloring sheets.

Lauren Wilford, who has worked in food service for 15 years, has noticed AI creeping into her recent interactions with guests as well. It started with the menu: Someone would upload a photo of it to ChatGPT or Claude and ask it what to order, or for guidance on a wine pairing, instead of asking the server.

But now, it appears, some customers have dropped the intermediary altogether. Over the past year, Wilford’s restaurant has been getting calls and emails from agents trying to make reservations on users’ behalf. The rise of agentic AI makes these interactions that much more confusing.

Wilford was surprised when a hands-off client suddenly became demanding on the eve of a big event, making last-minute requests for podiums and AV equipment — neither of which were readily available at the Providence, Rhode Island, restaurant she manages — and eleventh-hour changes to the catering menu. But Wilford was even more taken aback when the clients arrived the next day and didn’t mention any of it. Though she can’t prove it, Wilford believes the requests may not have come from anyone at the company at all; she suspects they were the work of an AI agent.

“I’m sympathetic to the reasons people use AI agents,” Wilford says, especially for bureaucratic and administrative tasks. “But anything where there’s value to two humans seeing each other and working something out together, I think we’re not sensitive to what might be lost if we try to skip all of that stuff.”

title: Gemini fully replaces Google Assistant on Android
snippet: At the start of September, the Google Assistant deprecation on mobile got underway. It now looks to be widely rolling out. more…
fullText:
At the start of September, the Google Assistant deprecation on mobile got underway. It now looks to be widely rolling out.

Google has been moving Assistant users to Gemini over the past few weeks. This deprecation was originally set for 2025 and later extended to 2026. In early August, Google announced the final timeline.

From various user reports today, this migration appears to be fully underway. Google Assistant is gone on all devices/accounts we checked in the US and Europe.

	

Notably, the Gemini app has removed the “Switch to Google Assistant” setting. This shortcut no longer appears at the bottom of the account menu with Google app 17.60 stable and 17.62 beta.

	

As such, you can no longer “use or switch back to Google Assistant on your phone, tablet, or paired devices.” The latter grouping includes Wear OS, headphones, and Android Auto.

There are no changes to Assistant just yet on “Google Nest and Google Home smart speakers, displays, or other Google Assistant-enabled speakers and displays.”

Gemini is now the “voice assistant experience on Android” when you long-press the power button or swipe from the corners.

title: Apple and Amazon face renewed UK antitrust lawsuit
snippet: A UK tribunal has allowed part of a renewed antitrust lawsuit against Apple and Amazon to move forward, over allegations that the companies restricted competition for Apple and Beats products sold on Amazon. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A UK tribunal has allowed part of a renewed antitrust lawsuit against Apple and Amazon to move forward, over allegations that the companies restricted competition for Apple and Beats products sold on Amazon. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Back in 2023, Apple and Amazon were hit with a proposed UK class action over a 2018 agreement that allegedly restricted which third-party sellers could offer Apple and Beats products through Amazon’s marketplace, reducing competition and, as a result, driving up prices for consumers.

It is worth noting that the UK was not the only market where the agreement drew scrutiny. Apple and Amazon have faced antitrust investigations and legal challenges over similar reseller restrictions in countries including Italy, Spain, Germany, and the United States.

In the British lawsuit, a class representative led by consumer law academic Christine Riefa accused the companies of reducing competition and driving up prices for consumers buying Apple and Beats products in the UK.

Last year, however, Britain’s Competition Appeal Tribunal refused to certify the case, citing concerns about how the lawsuit was being financed and about Riefa’s ability to independently protect the interests of the class.

The court took particular issue with the fact that, under the funding agreement, Asertis (which was financing the litigation in exchange for a success fee) could potentially have been paid out of any damages award before consumers received anything. The tribunal said the arrangement could even have resulted in the class receiving no damages at all.

From the decision:

“Our overall impression was that Prof Riefa was extremely reliant on her legal

advisers. We were not convinced that she had properly understood the

arrangements into which the PCR had entered on behalf of the Proposed Class

Members, and we were concerned about her ability to protect the interests of

the class robustly and independently.”

And

“Our key concern in this case is that Prof Riefa has not demonstrated sufficient

independence or robustness so as to act fairly and adequately in the interests of

the class.”

In its conclusion, the tribunal said a class representative cannot be “merely a figurehead” for proceedings being conducted by their lawyers, and that they should “act as the independent advocate for the class.”

The claim was later refiled by a new proposed class representative, Justin Le Patourel, which brings us to today.

UK tribunal allows part of lawsuit to proceed

As reported by Reuters, Britain’s Competition Appeal Tribunal today allowed part of the refiled lawsuit to proceed, while narrowing the case to claims involving Apple products purchased through Amazon’s marketplace.

From Reuters:

The tribunal allowed claims ​relating to Apple products bought through Amazon’s marketplace to proceed, but rejected ⁠one covering those bought directly from Apple and other retailers.

And

Judge Kelyn Bacon said claims relating to Amazon marketplace purchases were “plausible, credible ‌and ⁠grounded in the facts”, but rejected wider claims relating to other retailers because they rested on a “complex and speculative theory of harm”.

Reuters says the portion of the lawsuit now allowed to proceed could be worth between £289 million and £306 million, including interest.

Commenting on the decision, Apple told Reuters that its agreement with Amazon was intended to curb the sale of counterfeit products, and maintained that it “strongly” disagrees with the lawsuit.

Amazon, in turn, said it is confident the remaining claim will prove to be “without merit” as the legal process moves forward.

Finally, Reuters says a spokesperson for Le Patourel “welcomed the ruling, but said it was disappointing ​that parts ⁠of the claim were not certified.”

title: Bose launched wired, yes, wired, earbuds with ANC for $99
snippet: The new Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds connect via USB-C and work with almost any device. more…
fullText:
The new Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds connect via USB-C and work with almost any device.

Bose wants to get back to basics, it seems – it just launched a new pair of wired earbuds with ANC, citing a rise in wired listening popularity. The earbuds connect to any USB-C device, using an internal, proprietary DSP to ensure they work in just about any USB-C port. With any source input, the earbuds output a fixed 24bit signal.

Bose is well-known for its Quiet Comfort lineup in recent years, but it didn’t start there. Still, the company can be considered one of the main players responsible for quality ANC in wireless headphones. After all, the QC35’s became the go-to travel option for some time.

This release, however, has literal strings attached. It needs USB-C to operate, not a 3.5mm output as most wired enthusiasts prefer at a minimum. That means you wouldn’t be able to use your own DAC/amp setup.

	

Even still, Bose’s Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds will be a good option for those who need ANC without the battery anxiety. Bose says the earbuds have two microphones on each bud to power active noise cancellation. Quiet Mode blocks most noise out, and Aware Mode acts as a transparency setting. ANC can also be disabled.

The new wired Bose earbuds are available to pre-order starting today for $99 in Black and White Smoke. Bose says the buds will begin shipping on October 15 for those who order from the official website and Best Buy.

title: Google confirms Photos bug that prevents editing and deleting, fix coming ‘ASAP’
snippet: Google Photos is undoubtedly the best way to manage your photo library on Android and beyond, but a recent bug has been stopping users from being able to commit even the most basic of tasks, including sharing, editing, and even delete images from their collection. Luckily, if you’ve found yourself dealing with these issues, Google has confirmed a fix is on the way. more…
fullText:
Google Photos is undoubtedly the best way to manage your photo library on Android and beyond, but a recent bug has been stopping users from being able to commit even the most basic of tasks, including sharing, editing, and even delete images from their collection. Luckily, if you’ve found yourself dealing with these issues, Google has confirmed a fix is on the way.

Various user reports on Reddit last week confirmed that a recent glitch has been preventing users from interacting with images after they’ve been edited. That includes sharing, adding to galleries, deleting, and re-editing photos, all from changes as simple as cropping an image. Luckily, Google confirmed in a statement with Android Authority — which reported on the app issues late last week — that a fix is being worked on, with the team working to roll it out “ASAP.”

The Google Photos team is working on rolling out a fix ASAP! […] For now, users can try these 2 workarounds: 1) Tap “Save as copy” when saving new edits, and 2) Visit photos.google.com to delete or share already-edited photos.

Until these changes are live, the company recommends either saving your image as a copy when creating new edits (to prevent locking up the original, sole copy of an image) or accessing the web version of Photos to share or delete as needed.

While I can’t say I’ve seen this bug on my own Pixel 11 Pro XL, it does appear that most of the affected users — or at least those reporting the issue online — are sporting the last few generations of Google’s Tensor-powered devices. If you’ve found yourself in that group, keep an eye on the Play Store for an update coming soon.

title: MacBook Pro redesign is coming, with three features we’ve waited years for
snippet: Apple has a big MacBook Pro redesign in the works (possibly called MacBook Ultra) that’s expected to launch in October. Here are three rumored new features that we’ve waited a long time for. more…
fullText:
Apple has a big MacBook Pro redesign in the works (possibly called MacBook Ultra) that’s expected to launch in October. Here are three rumored new features that we’ve waited a long time for.

#1: OLED display

It’s hard to overstate the value of display technology for a product that many users spend all day looking at. Yet for years, the Mac has lagged behind Apple’s other products in offering the most cutting-edge display tech.

OLED has been a mainstay on iPhone for years, and iPad Pro introduced a tandem OLED in 2024 that many Mac users pined for. Now with the new MacBook Pro, OLED is finally coming to Mac.

The redesigned MacBook Pro with OLED is expected to offer truer blacks, improved contrast, and likely help out with battery life too. Here’s hoping it’s able to match the impressive tandem OLED the iPad offers.

#2: Touchscreen

Apple has long argued that the Mac doesn’t need a touchscreen, despite competing products nearly all offering touch. But rumors indicate we’re finally getting the first Mac with touch support.

The new MacBook Pro will have a touchscreen, and macOS 27 is already packed with hints that such a feature is coming. We’re expecting further software optimizations to make touch feel like a natural experience on the Mac.

Despite touch being available, macOS will remain tailored primarily for trackpad and keyboard input. Touch will be a secondary tool on the Mac, not replacing traditional input methods but rather supplementing them for users who have grown accustomed to touchscreens on iPhones, iPads, and PCs.

#3: No more notch

When Apple last redesigned the MacBook Pro in 2021, it introduced a notch design that first came to iPhone. The notch then spread to the MacBook Air too, making it a fixture of modern Mac design.

	

But the new MacBook Pro will reportedly drop the notch in favor of a hole-punch camera cutout that likely resembles what we’ve seen on iPhone Duo.

The Dynamic Island will be brought over to macOS too, making the camera cutout integrate seamlessly on the Mac like it does on iPhone. As someone who finds the notch more of an eyesore on the Mac than I ever did on iPhone, I’m excited to see the notch disappear soon.

title: Google combines Material 3 Expressive & Liquid Glass on the iPhone [Gallery]
snippet: With Liquid Glass now a year old, Google apps on iOS are beginning to incorporate the translucent material alongside its Material 3 Expressive design language. more…
fullText:
With Liquid Glass now a year old, Google apps on iOS are beginning to incorporate the translucent material alongside its Material 3 Expressive design language.

Previously, the Google Photos floating bottom bar on iOS had a solid background, just like the Android version. As of version 7.94, it’s now made of Liquid Glass.

The screenshots on the left show the “Default” translucency level, while the “More clear” option is on the right and lets you see more of the image behind it. With the dark theme, you see how the default blue accent color tints the current tab indicator.

Google has also updated buttons in the top bar with Liquid Glass.

	

The traditional bottom bar in Google Health has also been updated with Liquid Glass. You can see what’s under the navigation element, while the “Ask Coach” FAB (floating action button) gets a frosted treatment.

The company is still in the process of phasing out the previous Google Material Theme design language on iOS with Material 3. Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, and Keep have been stragglers, while Tasks was updated fairly recently.

More broadly, Google has shown no interest in adding Dynamic Color to its iOS apps. It could add a manual system that lets users choose an accent color across all Google apps. That said, without system access to the wallpaper, it’s a bit pointless, with Dynamic Color always more of a system-level Android feature.

title: ‘Carrie’ Review: Mike Flanagan’s Remake Is a Timely (and Terrifying) High School Tragedy
snippet: Prime Video’s Carrie is a poignant, emotional retelling of Stephen King’s classic horror story.
fullText:
There’s a new Carrie in town. The upcoming horror series from Executive Producer Mike Flanagan (creator and director of Netflix’s The Haunting of Hill House) aims to introduce the tragedy of young Carrie White to a new audience while offering die-hard fans a new perspective. All eight episodes land on Wednesday on Prime Video, and I’m sure the heated fan discussions will follow.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma’s movie adaptation of Stephen King‘s debut novel hit theaters. Carrie follows the story of a misunderstood girl with psychic abilities who is bullied at school and abused at home until things come to a bloody and fiery end. The film made Sissy Spacek a star, turned King’s book into a bestseller and set the stage for him to become the prolific, iconic genre writer we know today.

Read more: Prime Video: The 31 Absolute Best Shows to Watch

			

More from CNET

This isn’t the first reincarnation of the Carry White story. There was a sequel, two movie remakes and even a stage musical all inspired by her story. Now, it’s Flanagan’s turn to tell the tale, and the result is a layered, in-depth study of how grief and trauma can shape and destroy a strong mother-daughter bond.

Summer H. Howell and Samantha Sloyan as Carrie and Margaret White in Prime Video’s Carrie.Liane Hentscher/Prime Video

Further, it’s an exploration of how a broken education system and unchecked abuse, through social media of all things, can lead to the unraveling of an awkward girl who just wants to exist in a world that shuns her at every turn.

The first big departure for the show from the movie is its narrative structure. De Palma’s movie runs 98 minutes; Flanagan’s series is roughly three times longer, which gives the story a chance to breathe and allows him to expand on the overall world it takes place in.

As I mentioned above, school plays a huge part in the series. We get insight into the lives of the faculty, their struggles in teaching the students, while also balancing their own demons. And since it is modern-day, there’s an assortment of added details like social media bullying and interference from strong-willed parents.

I regularly imagine what my own high school experience would’ve been like if everyone had a smartphone in their pocket, ready at a moment’s notice to record someone being bullied and share it online. That’s a big component here, and, without spoiling much, it is an instigator, sparking the fire in Carrie that inevitably leads to the bloody climax at prom. However, there are also tributaries that extend from this social media abuse that impact the high school and the community at large.

High school showers are the worst.Prime Video

If you’re at all familiar with Flanagan’s work, you’ll know he is attracted to emotionally deep stories. His version of Carrie spends a lot of time establishing the relationship between Carrie and her mother, Margaret White, who, in the original movie and book, is presented as an evil religious zealot. Piper Laurie’s performance as Carrie’s mom is iconic, unhinged and downright terrifying.

Instead of going in that direction, here, this iteration of Carrie builds a complicated, loving relationship between mother and daughter. The introduction of school and the outside world leads to a breakdown of that bond, as Carrie begins to discover and eventually lean into her power.

Summer H. Howell’s performance as Carrie is utterly heartbreaking. Her ability to wear her emotions on her sleeve and cycle between childlike innocence and unbridled rage is the necessary energy that steers the series where it needs to go. She’s simply transcendent in the role. 

When did Margaret White become the voice of reason anyway?

Samantha Sloyan’s take on Margaret White is an absolute surprise, though. I knew going into this that she’d deliver a memorable performance, considering the work she did as devout zealot Bev Keane in Flanagan’s Netflix series, Midnight Mass. She brings a similar energy to the role of Margaret, but instead of dialing up the god-fearing madness, this version of the character is delightfully nuanced.

I found myself relating to her and even rooting for her, which wasn’t something I had on my bingo card going into this.

As for Carrie’s peers, the ensemble cast delivers. Sierra Agudong’s Sue Snell offers a conflicted voice of reason amid the unfolding madness. Alison Thornton’s exploration of Chris Hargensen is filled with sadness and an unfettered thirst for power, as her semblance of normalcy crumbles.

Just two high school girls hanging out, not doing anything troubling at all.Robert Falconer/Prime Video

Young female relationships populate the series, which has led to concerns I’ve read online that this will once again be a Carrie told through a male’s eyes. Yes, Flanagan’s name is on the project and, yes, King is the one who penned the original tale, but a lot has changed since the De Palma movie first premiered. 

His film still holds a place in cinema, but all you need to do is revisit the famed locker room scene in which Carrie gets her first period, and you’ll see a lot of nudity, which is troubling, considering the fact that these women (actresses all of legal age) were still portraying underage high school girls.

Aside from Flanagan contributing as a writer and director on the series, Prime Video’s Carrie features an array of female writers (Elizabeth Padden, Justina Ireland, Dani Parker, Alexandra Magistso and Rebecca Leigh Klingel) and directors (Kate Siegel, Axelle Carolyn, Kyra Sedgwick and Hiromi Kamata), which gives the story a new perspective. 

Finally, the tragedy of Carrie White is told through a necessary female gaze, and, in the process, the conflicts that arise resonate on a deeper, more authentic level.

By the time we get to the prom, the storm of blood, fire and death hits in a much different, impactful way.

Carrie is technically a horror series, but there’s a lack of gore and violence featured throughout most of the series. That may sound like a flaw, but it’s a detail that only adds to the emotional experience. Take away the supernatural aspect of the story, and you’d be left with a poignant coming-of-age tragedy that ticks all the binge-worthy boxes of a streaming series worthy of your time. But this is a Mike Flanagan joint, so what else are you expecting?

title: Samsung’s open-ear Galaxy Buds On go official with late October release
snippet: Samsung has officially announced its first truly open-ear Galaxy Buds with the Galaxy Buds On set for a debut in late October. more…
fullText:
Samsung has officially announced its first truly open-ear Galaxy Buds with the Galaxy Buds On set for a debut in late October.

Announced on its newsroom in Korea, Samsung’s Galaxy Buds On are a pair of clip-style earbuds. Made popular by a host of other brands, this design clips onto the side of your ear, positioning the driver into your ear but leaving room for ambient sounds to come through.

Samsung says you can interact with Galaxy Buds On via “a light touch” at the back half of the earbuds while they also feature automatic volume adjustments, actively work to reduce noise leakage, and have upgrade call quality too. The whole thing runs on a Snapdragon chip and packs 9.5 hours of battery life. 

Gemini Live is supported, just like on Samsung’s other recent Galaxy Buds, and there are also head gestures to answer or end calls, dismiss alarms, and more. 

	

The charging case is essentially identical to the one used on Galaxy Buds 4.

It sounds like they will not be cheap. In Korea, they’ll sell for 299,000 won, which is over $200 USD. The release date in Korea is October 27 with global markets “thereafter.”

title: Amazon’s new Fire TV Stick 4K ditches Android & sideloading for $59.99
snippet: Amazon continues its move away from Android on Fire TV, with its latest Fire TV Stick 4K moving over to Vega OS, though with upgrades including support for using your TV’s USB port for power and a massively improved remote. more…
fullText:
Amazon continues its move away from Android on Fire TV, with its latest Fire TV Stick 4K moving over to Vega OS, though with upgrades including support for using your TV’s USB port for power and a massively improved remote.

Available starting today, the new Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K costs $59.99 – $29.99 as a part of Prime Day deals next week. The new streamer, Amazon touts, is around 20-40% faster in most tasks compared to other 4K streaming devices and TVs while also being smaller than prior generations.

One welcome upgrade here is that you can power the new Fire TV Stick 4K using your TV’s USB port, making it a whole lot easier to power the streamer.

Amazon is also debuting a new remote here which has an asymmetric design that’s flat on top and rounded at the bottom. It has a metal home button for easy recognition, a customizable Star button, and IR controls for your other TV hardware such as a soundbar. Amazon is also launching a standalone version of this remote for other Fire TV devices.

	

The big change compared to the last generation, though, is that the latest Fire TV Stick 4K ditches Android in favor of Vega OS. Amazon’s new platform is indeed faster and continues to add more apps in time – Amazon says over 2,000 apps have been added this year – but it also loses support for sideloading, a popular option among many Fire TV users.

As mentioned, the new Fire TV Stick costs $59.99 and is available for purchase starting today in the US.

title: Google aware of Android Auto bug that blocks calls if your foldable phone is closed
snippet: An Android Auto bug is reportedly blocking outgoing calls from closed foldable phones, like the Motorola Razr. Both Google and Motorola are aware of the issue, which might mean a fix for those affected soon. more…
fullText:
An Android Auto bug is reportedly blocking outgoing calls from closed foldable phones, like the Motorola Razr. Both Google and Motorola are aware of the issue, which might mean a fix for those affected soon.

There is no shortage of form factors in the bucket of Android foldable devices. The most iconic might be the Razr from Motorola, if only for the nostalgia associated with it. Just like the original Razr flip phone in the mid-2000s, and every other foldable, the outer display has at least some use cases. Making or taking calls is a big one.

According to a couple of reports on Motorola and Google forums, the Motorola Razr can’t actually make calls while the phone is closed and connected to Android Auto because of a strange bug (via Android Authority). If an outgoing call is attempted, Android Auto throws an error that suggests opening the phone. When open, outgoing calls go through without issue.

Obviously, that negates the benefit of having a foldable device. And storing your foldable phone somewhere in your car while the internal display is exposed might be neglect, at least, in line with Samsung and Motorola’s suggested care.

	

The bug reports only mention calling from a Motorola Razr connected to Android Auto, ranging from the Razr Ultra 2025 and Razr Ultra 2026.

According to those users, there is a fix. The good news – reverting back to Google Assistant from Gemini solves the problem. The bad news – Google Assistant was just fully removed from Android as a whole on September 28.

Both Google and Motorola are aware of the Android Auto bug. Motorola’s thread lists a response from the company less than two weeks ago. It’s possible the bug is still affecting users, and with Gemini taking over for Google Assistant, the issue might only spread to more users and devices until a fix is widely rolled out.

Are you able to make Android Auto calls while your foldable phone is closed? Or is it working now?

title: Huawei’s Mate 90 Pro Max says ‘why not’ and just lets you add an entire camera
snippet: Huawei has just introduced its new Mate 90 Pro Max in China and the big feature is not the cameras built into the device, but rather the giant one you can add on. more…
fullText:
Huawei has just introduced its new Mate 90 Pro Max in China and the big feature is not the cameras built into the device, but rather the giant one you can add on.

The Huawei Mate 90 Pro Max is the company’s latest flagship, packing a 6.9-inch dual-layer OLED display, Huawei’s in-house Kirin 9050 (or Pro) chip, Harmony OS 7.0, 12GB or 16GB of RAM, a 6,800 mAh battery, IP68/69, and a pretty solid camera setup. The main camera is a 50MP shooter with variable aperture, backed up by a 40MP ultrawide and a 200MP telephoto shooter with 4x optical zoom.

There’s also a 13MP front-facing camera with a 3D depth sensor, split into three different camera cutouts.

It’s not the phone itself that’s so attention-grabbing, though.

	

Huawei has a “Z10” camera module add-on that’s basically just an entire camera you can attach to the phone. It packs a 1-inch camera sensor, up to 10x optical zoom, and a huge detachable lens. Huawei explains (translated):

A multi-lens optical system, a 24mm-240mm focal length, 10x continuous optical zoom, and a  maximum aperture of F2.0-F4.5, combined with a 1-inch sensor, delivers superior imaging capabilities. 

The innovative HyperClick mount allows for a seamless connection to your phone with a single click, enabling instant sharing after shooting – making travel photography incredibly convenient. It naturally captures portrait interactions and realistically reproduces distant skylines, making professional imaging capabilities readily available.

Like the built-in cameras, which the module covers up, this add-on camera uses an RYYB sensor, and it’s a 50MP sensor. It can adjust between a 24mm and 240mm focal length.

The cost of the add-on “Z10” camera is 5,999 CNY, around $900 USD. The Huawei Mate 90 Pro Max itself runs 9,499 CNY, around $1,400. Both are available this week in China.

fullText:

The Last First: Winter K2

When: October 2

What: Movie

Genre: Documentary

In “The Last First: Winter K2,” Amir Bar-Lev tells a complex, harrowing and moving story that unpacks the industry of extreme mountain climbing and its changing culture. Focusing on a 2021 expedition, mountaineers John Snorri Sigurjónsson, an Icelander, and the Pakistani father-son team of Ali and Sajid Sadpara set out to be the first to summit K2 in the winter, when the mountain’s conditions are the cruelest. The men soon find themselves sharing the treacherous ascent with influencer climbers and their film crews, commercial expedition clients and Nims, a Nepalese celebrity mountaineer, and his team of Sherpas. “The Last First: Winter K2” takes us to the icy heights and unpredictable weather of K2 and reveals a surprising and layered story — one of strategy and determination, class and caste, money and power — all under life and death circumstances.

title: Amazon will give you up to $275 extra to buy a Pixel 11 right now
snippet: Through a boosted trade-in deal, Amazon will give Pixel 11 series buyers an extra $275 towards their new device. more…
fullText:
Through a boosted trade-in deal, Amazon will give Pixel 11 series buyers an extra $275 towards their new device.

Amazon has been more heavily pushing trade-in offers over the past year, with the Pixel 11 series being a great example. During pre-orders, the online retail behemoth would offer hundreds of dollars on top of existing trade-in values when buying one of Google’s new devices, and that’s still happening.

At the moment, Amazon is offering a $275 boost to any trade-in towards a Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, or Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Trade-in values are advertised as maxing out around $850, though most recent devices fall into the $500~ range. But the real benefit here is that you can get the extra credit applied even on older devices that aren’t worth as much. The trade-in boost varies from device to device, but there are still some good deals to be had here.

A few examples we put together include:

As you can see, there are’t a ton of devices that get the full $275 boost, and there’s also not much rhyme or reason to why certain devices get a boost or a different value than others. Still, if you’re looking at buying a Pixel 11 device, it’s a deal worth taking a look at. title: Blender, the 3D modeling app, is launching for Android next year; iPad app still on pause
snippet: One of the biggest headaches facing Google’s push to make Android more of a desktop platform is the professional sector of apps and programs, but one big name is making the effort, as Blender is working to bring its app to Android. more…
fullText:
One of the biggest headaches facing Google’s push to make Android more of a desktop platform is the professional sector of apps and programs, but one big name is making the effort, as Blender is working to bring its app to Android.

Blender is an industry-recognized suite of tools used for 3D modeling. It’s effectively the go-to option, and for good reason. 

Shown off at the Blender Conference 2026, Blender is making the effort to bring its app to Android. The hour-long video goes over the details of how the app works and the roadmap for releasing the port, which is targeting a release in the first half of 2027. An APK demo is already available. The port appears to be mainly focused on tablets, which is a bigger undertaking than you might think. Blender relies quite heavily on keyboard shortcuts, so bringing a fully functional experience on a touchscreen is a massive change. It appears that a stylus is a big part of the experience.

This comes at an important time, not only as Android tablets continue to advance, but also as Googlebook makes its debut. The Android-based platform opens up a new desktop-class platform for Blender.

	

Notably, iPad support for Blender is still “on hold” for the time being, despite the work for touchscreen support being brought to the Android app.

title: Apple Music 7.0 beta brings Liquid Glass redesign to Android
snippet: Apple Music for Android is getting a big Liquid Glass-inspired redesign with the latest 7.0 beta. more…
fullText:
Apple Music for Android is getting a big Liquid Glass-inspired redesign with the latest 7.0 beta.

With Liquid Glass now a year old on Apple platforms, the new design language is coming to Android. Apple Music now has a floating bottom bar that lets you see what is above, below, and to the sides. The navigation element has a small amount of translucency that allows you to mostly see solid colors underneath.

Old vs. new

Similarly, the mini-player above it gets the same treatment and is no longer docked with the bottom bar. Compared to Liquid Glass on iOS, scrolling does not collapse the bar into a more compact version, with everything remaining in place.

	

Top bars across the app have been updated, with the page title and overflow menu on the same line. The three-dot icons are no longer themed red and have been placed in circular containers. The Library tab sees the biggest update with “Edit Pins” and “Edit Categories” now part of the overflow.

Artist pages get a big update with the background now themed based on the cover image. This closely matches the iOS design with a more prominent play button and info page that’s no longer at the very bottom. Share has also been placed in the top-right corner.

	

The Settings page has also been modernized with better grouping. There are no major changes to Now Playing, which did not see any big updates on iOS.

Finally, Apple Music 7.0 now has an edge-to-edge design for the status and navigation bars.

With the last release, Apple Music for Android switched to a new versioning system that aligns with iOS. Today’s version 7.0 aligns with iOS 27.

Apple Music 7.0 is currently in beta, with testing usually lasting a few weeks. You can sign up from the Play Store listing or this page. In general, these builds are fairly stable.

title: The clever way Apple embedded Face ID beneath the iPhone 18 Pro screen
snippet: In the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken one of the next steps toward its long-term vision of the iPhone as a single slab of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display. Achieving this without having the Face ID array be visible through the display and without compromising the quality of this section of the screen required some clever engineering … more…
fullText:
In the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken one of the next steps toward its long-term vision of the iPhone as a single slab of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display.

Achieving this without having the Face ID array be visible through the display and without compromising the quality of this section of the screen required some clever engineering …

Jony Ive described his long-term vision of the iPhone design as a single slab of glass, and while he is no longer with the company, that goal has remained. Eventually, Apple wants to embed all of the technology requiring screen real estate beneath the display, including both Face ID and front-facing camera.

The iPhone 18 Pro has achieved the first of these, but it was no easy task. Face ID requires infrared light to be both emitted and received by the TrueDepth module – and IR light cannot pass through display pixels.

Apple needed to create gaps between the pixels large enough to allow the IR light to pass between them, but without any visible degradation in the display. To do so, the company’s engineers set out to design a different pixel layout with larger gaps without visibly impacting what can be displayed on those pixels. 

iFixit used a microscope to show this pixel pattern, with Apple confirming to me me that the overall pixel density over the module is reduced by half. This would potentially have created a second problem: half the pixel density might have created a visibly dimmer section of the display, so Apple increases the brightness of these pixels to compensate. There also appears to be an IR pass filter to block visible light from passing through the gaps, further hiding the components.

The result is remarkable. For all practical purposes, the TrueDepth camera array is impossible to see even when staring at it extremely closely. I couldn’t capture it even using macro photography with different screen colors and lighting conditions. That’s not to say it’s completely impossible to detect, as iFixit’s microscope view shows, but rather that there is absolutely no way you’ll notice it in everyday use.

Right now, that achievement reduces the size of the Dynamic Island, which in turn enables support for three live activities rather than two. In some future iPhone model, the front-facing camera will also be hidden beneath the display. That’s technically possible today, but the compromise in image quality is currently greater than Apple is willing to accept. Solving that issue is a matter of when rather than if.

title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer Review: A Fantastic Burnout Successor From a Galaxy Far, Far Away
snippet: Developer Fuse Games’ debut release is one of the most impressive arcade racers in recent memory.
fullText:
It pains me to say it, but Star Wars’ cultural staying power has taken a massive blow in recent years – and for pretty good reason. Most of the Disney Plus shows have flopped, and the franchise’s return to cinema, The Mandalorian and Grogu, performed worse than any other theatrical release in the series’ history. Despite my lifelong fandom, I cast my eye upon the current state of the sci-fi space opera and feel a sense of apathy.

But Star Wars video games have remained consistently impressive in recent years – the Soulslike Jedi Fallen Order and Survivor duology and the turn-based Star Wars Zero Company were engaging entries in the canon, prioritizing fun gameplay over anything else.

Developer Fuse Games has continued this string of bangers across wildly different genres with Star Wars: Galactic Racer, an arcade-y game with speedy ships, plenty of underhanded action and a refreshingly self-contained story. It’s F-Zero meets Burnout, and it’s one of my new favorite racing games.

			

More from CNET

A classic underdog sports story with Star Wars set dressing

From the outset, I was uncertain if a plotline about a Star Wars racing league would remain narratively engaging over the course of an entire game — its spiritual predecessor, the 1999 podracing classic Star Wars Episode 1: Racer, didn’t bother with one. Once I found out Star Wars: Galactic Racer takes place between Return of the Jedi and The Force Awakens, I was even more skeptical – the sequel timeline hasn’t been an era for consistently engaging stories, after all.

It was a pleasant surprise, then, to discover that Galactic Racer tells a mostly novel story about a small corner of the universe coming to terms with a new normal after the downfall of the Galactic Empire. As it turns out, there’s not much time to engage with speeder racing when entire worlds are buckling under the tyranny of space fascism, so everything has to be put together again from the ground up.

Racing promoter Darius Pax has a passion for high-speed sports, and he’s wrangling sponsors for a new league by pulling in some of the best talent from across the galaxy. That includes shady characters like ex-TIE Fighter pilot Griff Halloran and kindhearted thrillseekers like old Soren Zaks. The most talented racer is nepo baby Kestar Bool, who is using his family’s riches to fund top-tier racing machines and initiate a hostile takeover of Pax’s assets. 

Players can choose among agile skim speeders like the one shown here, bulkier landspeeders or nimble speeder bikes.Fuse Games

To stave off the imminent threat of Bool seizing the league, Pax enlists the help of main character Shade and their happy-go-lucky mechanic Hibi to win the league championship and keep the sport pure. Shade has a devil-may-care attitude and a mysterious vendetta against the egoistic antagonist, so they’re happy enough to sign on to the competition.

The setup is your classic sports underdog story where you’re looking to score petty vengeance against your sneering opponent. There’s no high-stakes galaxy-level threat – this is a story about outperforming one bad guy on the most dangerous racetracks in the universe, and it rules.

Fuse Games describes the campaign structure as “runs-based,” which essentially means it plays out like many other roguelikes, where random rewards build up your kit as you progress up a procedurally generated tournament bracket. I’m not entirely sold on the integration of this concept for an arcade racer, but I appreciate how crashing out and losing too many events essentially scraps your vehicle and causes Shade and Hibi to begin anew. Shade is supposed to be a scrappy upstart, so losing your parts and upgrades and needing to retune the whole racing kit feels like it serves a narrative purpose.

The game features returns of some classic characters, and special modes where you can race their vehicles.Fuse Games

Galactic Racer does indulge in a little bit of nostalgia – Anakin’s podracing rival, Sebulba, appears as a washed-up legend, while the antagonistic Bool family apparently built a large chunk of its wealth running part of the empire’s slave trade. There are plenty of cameos and one-off dialogue lines that will tickle lore nerds pink.

Still, there’s more restraint in this game’s storytelling than in most Star Wars projects, and the narrative is better off for it. I think fans want to explore new corners of the galaxy rather than follow the same handful of bloodlines – I know I do – and Galactic Racer debuts plenty of fun characters that don’t connect to high-stakes galaxy-ending plotlines.

The seedy underbelly of the Star Wars universe is perhaps the space opera at its most entertaining, even if that wretched hive of scum and villainy is largely composed of comically evil mobsters and smugglers. It’s great fun to explore that side of the sci-fi world without forcibly including a legacy character like Han Solo or Boba Fett.

Scrappy, speedy and strategic playstyles are equally viable

There’s a surprising amount of depth to Galactic Racer’s build system. Before you even start a run, you need to decide whether you’re flying a versatile landspeeder, risky speeder bike or graceful skim speeder – each vehicle has different acceleration speeds, turning rates and drifting capabilities.

You’ll start a campaign tournament with mostly stock equipment, but each race won provides credits and upgrades that will help you prepare for the knockout championship event. Different parts provide passive bonuses on the track, and active abilities let you expend the vehicle’s energy at key moments to score advantages in a race.

As with any roguelike, I found a build type that worked for me: I routinely invest in my speeder’s afterburners and its volatile ramjet engine, picking up parts that permit boosting in the dangerous redline zone for longer before worrying about blowing up my craft. There’s still an appreciable level of friction that forces players to make hard decisions – you’re not guaranteed to find parts or abilities you like to use, and crashing or corroding your ship during races can do damage that carries debuffs over to the next event.

More kinetic abilities that encourage brawls with other racers are probably going to be fan favorites, because Galactic Racer has a sickly satisfying takedown system ripped straight out of the old Burnout games. Brushing up against other speeders and watching the sparks fly feels intense, and slamming into an opponent will reward you with a crash cam as they go careening off the track. This type of carnage may not win every run, but building a resilient chassis or dropping bombs to cause mayhem is absolutely cathartic.

That’s not to say that I’m completely in love with every ability you can pick up in the game. The addition of an autopilot is particularly silly to me, especially since drifting around sharp turns and racing clean lines feels gratifying. Worse, while it might buy a couple of seconds to activate traps or fix malfunctioning parts, the ability could just as easily betray you by ending right before you speed directly into a wall. It just isn’t particularly well-implemented – but that’s one of the exceedingly few balancing missteps I discovered.

Lots of thought was put into the roguelike structure of Galactic Racer, and it feels like there’s a viable path for every type of racer to win – whether you enjoy running clean lines or using underhanded tactics to force opponents off the track.

This arcade racer can go the distance

There’s plenty of content for budding racers to take on once they’ve taken Kestar Bool down a few pegs in Galactic Racer’s story mode. The game features arcade time trials, multiplayer races, podracing events and more cosmetic rewards than you can shake a rathtar tentacle at. These are genuinely challenging races that could take hours to score a gold medal on, and I started to feel like a bit of a masochist after half a dozen attempts to master the ramjet-themed arcade event.

A notable pain point is the lack of an AI quick race – it seems like a massive oversight that there’s no mode where you can hop on, pick a track and difficulty and duke it out in a single match against some bots. This is something that I hope gets rectified soon.

A few flaws notwithstanding, it’s obvious that the development team at Fuse Games has an earnest love for this storied universe, and it shows through plenty of little tidbits and extra flourishes that flesh out the gameplay experience. Runs build into their own diegetic narratives as players crash out opponents and form rivalries that last throughout multiple races.

Characters react to your skill (or lack thereof), challenging Shade to one-on-one knockout races and proposing lucrative sidebets before each event. It makes sense that any headstrong individual willing to strap themselves into a speeder bike and speed through the wreckage of a downed Star Destroyer would arrogantly put their money where their mouth is, and it makes the world feel alive.

Many of those elements carry over to the multiplayer tours, where players are able to gamble among themselves with credits earned in previous races – I can foresee this potentially getting a tad toxic in a public lobby, but in my experience, it was a great way for emergent narratives to form and made the mode feel all the more meaningful.

I can’t imagine this game will make many critics’ GOTY lists, especially when so many blockbuster projects have already been released. But Star Wars: Galactic Racer is easily one of my favorite games of 2026 – and not just because its gameplay loop had me inadvertently staying up for “one more run” at 3 a.m.

Among its many virtues, the game reminded me that there’s still value in a galaxy far, far away. Over breakneck races and loving details, my apathy for the series melted away, returning a childlike spark of awe and wonder for this sci-fi universe. I doubt a game like this will dictate the future creative direction of a juggernaut franchise like Star Wars, but Galactic Racer is surely something special for anyone who wants to ride their ramjet from Crait to Tatooine.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is set to be released for PlayStation 5, Windows and Xbox Series X/S on Tuesday.
excerpt:
It pains me to say it, but Star Wars’ cultural staying power has taken a massive blow in recent years – and for pretty good reason. Most of the Disney Plus shows have flopped, and the franchise’s return to cinema, The Mandalorian and Grogu, performed worse than any other theatrical release in the series’ history. Despite my lifelong fandom, I cast my eye upon the current state of the sci-fi space opera and feel a sense of apathy.

But Star Wars video games have remained consistently impressive in recent years – the Soulslike Jedi Fallen Order and Survivor duology and the turn-based Star Wars Zero Company were engaging entries in the canon, prioritizing fun gameplay over anything else.

While he dreams only of becoming the most famous chef in the world, his talent and ambitions attract the attention of renowned and powerful politicians who use him as a spy for France. Determined to escape poverty and fulfill his dream, Carême can choose revenge or he can have it all — women, wealth, fame — but at what cost? His love? His soul? His life?

If you haven’t done it before, I highly recommend the ‘Get ready’ process to anyone ordering directly from Apple. It’s a great way to minimize potential hiccups on the morning of pre-orders, which means you’ll have a better chance of launch day delivery.

title: Honor Magic 9 Pro Max goes official with 8,800 mAh battery, ARRI cameras, Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
snippet: Honor has officially announced its latest flagship in China, with the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max packing powerful specs, upgraded cameras, the latest Snapdragon chip, and confirmed for an global launch later on. more…
fullText:
Honor has officially announced its latest flagship in China, with the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max packing powerful specs, upgraded cameras, the latest Snapdragon chip, and confirmed for an global launch later on.

The Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is an all-out flagship with a heavy focus on its cameras, so let’s start there.

Continuing its ARRI partnership that debuted on the Robot Phone, the Magic 9 Pro Max packs a 200MP main camera with “gimbal-level stabilization,” a 200MP telephoto camera with 3.5x optical zoom, and a 50MP ultra-wide camera. Those are arranged on the back in the style of an ARRI cinema camera, and they’re also tuned by ARRI to produce better colors both in photos and videos. Honor is also building out additional hardware including two teleconverter lenses and a “Mobile Video Kit” in partnership with SmallRig.

The front-facing camera is no slouch either, with a 55MP sensor that’s paired with a 3D depth sensing camera for face unlock.

	

The phone surrounding those cameras packs a punch too. 

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and starts at 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. Honor is using its own “Imaging Chip H1” to enhance camera processing, with MagicOS 11 based on Android 17 also available out of the box (with all its Liquid Glass-y-ness). The display is a 6.8-inch 2868×1320 OLED panel with Honor’s NanoCrystal Shield on top (which is both anti-scratch and anti-reflective), 10,000 nits of peak brightness – somehow –, 1-120Hz adaptive refresh rate support, and a 4,320Hz PWM dimming rate for better eye comfort. There’s an 8,800 mAh battery inside with 100W wired charging and 80W wireless, and the whole phone has IP68, IP69, and IP69K dust/water resistance ratings. 

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max specs

6.8-inch 2868×1320 LTPO OLED display, NanoCrystal glass, 4,320Hz PWM, 10,000 nits peak brightness

Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

12/256GB, 12/512GB, 16/512GB, 16/1TB

MagicOS 11 based on Android 17

Rear Cameras: 200MP main (f/1.57), 200MP telephoto (f/2.6, 3.5x optical zoom, up to 200x digital zoom), 50MP ultrawide with autofocus

Front Camera: 55MP + 3D depth-sensing camera

8,800 mAh battery, 100W wired charging, 80W wireless charging

IP68/IP69/IP69K

The Magic 9 Pro Max is available today in China, but Honor says global availability is coming soon. Europe, MEA (Middle East & Africa), SEA (Southeast Asia), and “other key international markets” are all confirmed at this point, but there’s no reason to expect this one in the US. 

Honor also launched the Magic 9 in China.

It has a similar design but with a smaller 6.37-inch display, Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, a very similar camera array, and an 8,000 mAh battery.

title: John Ternus has big plans to make Apple ‘leaner’ and release more products
snippet: New CEO John Ternus has plans to “overhaul” Apple in an attempt to make it “run faster and leaner,” according to a new report from Bloomberg. This includes introducing more products, eliminating “middle-management positions,” and much more. more…
fullText:
New CEO John Ternus has plans to “overhaul” Apple in an attempt to make it “run faster and leaner,” according to a new report from Bloomberg. This includes introducing more products, eliminating “middle-management positions,” and much more.

John Ternus wants to reshape Apple, here’s how

First, the new Apple CEO wants to release more products faster than before, including becoming “more experimental.” One idea is to shake up Apple’s release calendar and rely less on the typical spring-and-fall cadence, instead releasing more new products throughout the year. 

Ternus also wants to “create a leaner organization with a greater focus on engineering.” This includes several cost-cutting measures and restructuring. For instance, one change is “eliminating some middle-management positions to reduce the layers separating engineers from senior executives.”

The report says Apple has dismissed “a number of engineering program managers, or EPMs,” in its hardware engineering division over the last two weeks. Bloomberg describes these roles as having been “central to Apple’s product-development process for decades,” responsible for “managing timelines and coordinating work across teams.”

“The cuts affected several program managers, including roughly half a dozen directors, one of the company’s most senior employee levels,” the report says. “Those employees were given just weeks to find other positions within Apple. Those who don’t secure new roles will be laid off later this year.”

Bloomberg says the cost-cutting measures could go much broader than that, though. Ternus has reportedly advocated for Apple to be “leaner” for years:

Ternus, 51, has advocated for a leaner organization for years. While leading hardware engineering, he told employees during an all-hands meeting that Apple should hire fewer people, ask more of its existing engineers and reduce organizational bloat. During a presentation, he showed a slide charting annual headcount growth and argued that the company should be accomplishing more with fewer employees.

Furthermore, Apple reportedly scrapped a plan over the summer to lay off 5,000 AppleCare employees, believing that AI-powered agents could handle those responsibilities.

At the same time, Ternus wants Apple to increase revenue from Apple’s services division alongside Eddy Cue and CFO Kevan Parekh. “They have discussed launching new services and extracting more revenue from existing products and offerings,” the report says.

Ultimately, one source told Bloomberg that things are “hectic” inside Apple right now:

“Everything is a lot more hands-on than it used to be,” said one person familiar with the situation. “It’s hectic right now.” That person and others said managers in product-development groups are being pushed to deliver more products, more frequently and on shorter timelines.

You can read the full report at Bloomberg. It’s a fascinating piece that I highly recommend reading in full.

title: iOS 27 brings three key new features to Find My
snippet: iOS 27 brings new features to almost all of Apple’s apps, including Messages, Apple Music, Wallet, and more. Apple’s Find My app has its own share of changes in iOS 27. Here’s everything new. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 brings new features to almost all of Apple’s apps, including Messages, Apple Music, Wallet, and more. Apple’s Find My app has its own share of changes in iOS 27. Here’s everything new.

iOS 27: What’s new for Find My?

Apple touts three changes to Find My in iOS 27:

More flexible sharing options

UI enhancements

Apple Watch updates

First, more flexible sharing options in Find My give you more control over when and for how long you share your location with others. “Share your location for a custom duration or until a set date and time,” Apple says. You can also now “pause sharing with people individually, whenever you want.”

One of the bigger changes here is that you can now hide your location from a specific person without sending them any notification or alert. The other person won’t be notified when you pause, stop, or resume sharing your location with them.

Previously, you could turn off your location in the Find My app altogether, which wouldn’t send a notification. This, however, hid your location from everyone. In iOS 27, you can disable your location for specific people. 

To manage this, you’ll see a new “Hide Location” toggle on each person’s card in the Find My app. If you pause sharing your location with someone, they will see a “No Location Found” message in their Find My app.

Design changes

As for the UI enhancements, Find My in iOS 27 has been refreshed with a new Liquid Glass interface. The app largely missed out on Liquid Glass in iOS 26, but this year it has a new tab bar design that matches Apple’s other apps.

The Find My interface now also shows more specific location information on the app’s main page. This means you don’t have to tap on each person to view exactly what street they’re on at any given moment.

There is also new iconography in the Find My app in iOS 27. The “Items” tab, for example, is now denoted by a new AirTag-style icon.

Apple Watch updates

Finally, for cellular Apple Watch users, sharing your location will automatically use your Apple Watch when you’re away from your iPhone or iPad. 

Also on Apple Watch, there’s a redesigned, unified Find My app that integrates people, items, and devices into one interface.

title: iPhone video stabilization continues to wow me in the iPhone 18 Pro
snippet: I first talked about how much iPhone video stabilization impressed me when I tested it on the iPhone 13 Pro back in 2021. It’s been improved significantly since then, with both the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro having a version Apple refers to as “ultra-stabilized video.” While it doesn’t sound as sexy as some features, it makes a massive difference to the usability of the iPhone for handheld shooting – and my latest test really drove home just how good it is today … more…
fullText:
I first talked about how much iPhone video stabilization impressed me when I tested it on the iPhone 13 Pro back in 2021. It’s been improved significantly since then, with both the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro having a version Apple refers to as “ultra-stabilized video.”

While it doesn’t sound as sexy as some features, it makes a massive difference to the usability of the iPhone for handheld shooting – and my latest test really drove home just how good it is today … 

I have a mini tripod and GorillaPod that I carry with me when I know I’m going to want to shoot some iPhone video footage, but of course, one of the huge benefits of an iPhone is that it’s the camera you always have with you. There are times when I spot an opportunity for a shot and don’t have a tripod with me. 

It’s often possible to improvise, whether that’s by leaning the iPhone against a railing or bracing myself against something like a lamppost. But there are times when I rely on the built-in video stabilization on iPhones, and in the most recent example, shooting with the iPhone 18 Pro, I was incredibly impressed. 

A riverboat trip down the Thames demonstrated that there are times when the iPhone’s built-in video stabilization feature is actually better than a tripod. That’s because the boat rocks around a fair bit, which would have meant a stable shot of the boat with the scenery outside moving around. The iPhone reliably stabilized to the outside world with the boat moving around in the foreground.

That ability to keep the horizon true no matter what movements the platform makes is something we don’t even get with a typical gimbal. Most consumer-grade ones smooth out movement rather than eliminating it. It’s only with high-end professional gimbals and the type of giro mount designed for marine and helicopter use that we get truly locked horizons.

The iPhone 18 Pro’s ultra-stabilization feature honestly delivers this level of performance, and that’s a pretty incredible feature to have as standard in the stock Camera app with no external hardware required.

Check out the sample footage below. If you don’t want to take the full ride, the Tower Bridge section starting here is probably the best showcase for the feature. But if you do want to enjoy the London tourist experience, hit C to switch on the captions for all the bridge names and a few other comments, including pointing out Apple’s UK campus.
