fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m going crazy over the NYT’s list of the best TV shows of the 21st century, redoing all of my vibe-projects with Opus 5.5, girding my loins for another Witcher 3 play-through now that the free remaster is out, and devouring Colson Whitehead’s new novel, Cool Machine.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

October 4th marks 10 years since Google debuted the Pixel, and over the next few days we plan to dive into the brand’s storied legacy. What started with a couple of HTC-built devices has expanded into an ecosystem that includes budget and flagship smartphones, smartwatches, earbuds, tablets, and more. 

	

The Pixel has served several purposes for Google throughout its lifespan, beginning as an extension of Nexus’s “Android best practices” before morphing into something a bit more complicated and abstract. When it debuted, Google emphasized the Pixel’s camera advantages, of which there were many, along with timely annual platform updates that arrived months before other Android devices.

As time went on, the Pixel brand came to encompass more than just smartphones; the company debuted its Tensor SoC inside the Pixel 6, and expanded the line to include the Pixel Watch, Pixel Buds, and a couple of failed Pixel-branded tablets. 

Perhaps the most remarkable thing about the Pixel lineup is its longevity; under Rick Osterloh, the brand has become synonymous with deep integration into Google’s services — of late, particularly Gemini — and a steward of thoughtful software and hardware design. The company’s products have made inroads in many markets, but still represent a single-digit share in most, including the US (despite solid year-over-year growth in 2026).

It’s perhaps also worth pointing out that the Pixel lineup has persevered in spite of many challenges, from major hardware issues with the Pixel 2 and 3 series to Covid-related supply constraints in the Pixel 5 to reputation-harming modem performance in the Pixel 6. It really wasn’t until 2023’s Pixel 8 series that Google shook its image as a mediocre hardware vendor and married superlative hardware with delightful software.

Today, the Pixel lineup is both the best and most predictable it’s ever been. The Pixel 11 series is yet another iteration on a design that debuted in 2021 with the Pixel 6. The Pixel Watch has looked identical since its 2022 debut. The Pixel Buds are fine but not competitive. The Pixel Tablet appears to be dead, and there’s no sign of a Pixelbook successor on the horizon.

Ten years in, is the Pixel brand where Google wanted it to be, with its cultural influence outpacing its financial viability? Perhaps not, but it’s also not likely to disappear anytime soon, which speaks volumes about its importance, both to the company and the community that keeps it in the conversation.

🤝 Cc: Max Weinbach

Welcome to Cc:, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, I’m speaking with Max Weinbach, who used to contribute to 9to5Google and is now a tech analyst with Creative Strategies.

Who are you?

I’m Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies. You might also know me from writing about phones at XDA and 9to5Google, or from spending way too much time talking about technology on Twitter.

What do you do for work?

I research and write about consumer technology, especially phones, PCs, chips, and AI. A lot of my work now is figuring out what AI can actually do when you give it a real task, real data, and the tools to finish the job. I also consider my job to be just knowing a lot about many different technology topics. 

That has turned into building things, too. We’ve been working on Diligence Stack and practical agent benchmarks, testing how the model, the tools, and the surrounding software affect the result. I want to know whether something can produce useful work and how much fixing it needs afterward. That tells me a lot more than a score by itself.

What do you do for fun?

I build things and play games. There’s quite a bit of overlap between my hobbies and my work. I’ll get interested in some software problem and end up with another side project. I’ve been spending a lot of time on native apps and experimenting with AI agents.

Reviewing gaming hardware is also a very convenient excuse to play something I’ve been putting off. That’s how I finally got around to Alan Wake 2 and picked Spider-Man 2 back up. 

On top of that, the classics of harassing playing with my dog and going to the gym. I’ve spent a lot of time learning about health and wellness. It’s just interesting to learn about and put into practice for me!

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

I’m still excited about it, but I care a lot about the experience of actually using something. A great spec sheet only gets you so far if the laptop is annoying, the software gets in your way, or the AI needs more supervision than the task was worth.

Some of my favorite products are the ones that are almost boring because they get the basics right. A comfortable laptop that runs the things I need, lasts a long time, and doesn’t have some weird deal-breaking issue is genuinely exciting to me. I’m also interested in how much easier it’s becoming to build the software I want to use.

What are three apps you can’t live without and why?

ChatGPT. I love ChatGPT as a product. It’s one of those apps that just let me kinda delegate whatever I want, and it will simply do it. It’s good for research, good for building one-off apps here and there, and just a great platform to help with anything I can think of. It doesn’t replace any actual work for me, but makes that work much easier and quicker. 

Whoop. Technically, an app and a product, but the product powers the app so I’m going with it. It’s one of my favorite ways to track health and wellness because it’s the first that has basically nailed the feeling of recovery and strain on a daily basis. In the morning I actually try to guess what the number will be based on what I feel, and I get it pretty close every morning. 

X/Twitter. X is one of my favorite ways to actually consume media and news, share my thoughts, keep up with friends. Yes, I know this is such a normal choice and nothing unique here, but I don’t know, I really like the app. My life would be very different without it.

What is a gadget that you love right now?

Plaud’s Note Pro MagSafe thing. It’s fantastic, and makes my life significantly easier all around when it comes to notes. I tend to have a good memory when it comes to meetings, so I tend to not take notes. That only gets you so far when it comes to specific details, and I find actually writing notes distracting. This thing solves it for me: take a recording, transcribe, and generate key notes while I can listen. Yes, voice memos exist on every phone and watch but I like this a lot more.

How does AI fit into your life right now?

It’s a big part of how I build and research things. I use agents for coding, testing ideas, and working through problems, then look at what they actually produce. The useful question for me is how close they get to a result I can use.

One recent example is having agents write and optimize Metal kernels for a local model, testing changes on the hardware as they go. I still choose between cloud and local models based on the job. Having the option to use both is valuable. 

I also have a ton of little ideas of how things should work, apps I want, little fun animations or widgets or whatever I can think of for my different products or phones or connecting to Siri and I can just make it by dictating into a magic box and an hour later it’s installed on my products.

What is a recent TV show you loved?

Lanterns, I think it’s just a fun good show that, while it’s not done yet, is just fun. It’s a superhero show that’s not a superhero show entirely. It’s simply a great story told extremely well with characters I like.

What is a recent game you loved?

Marvel’s Spider-Man 2. I bought a PS5 to play it and then never finished it, so reviewing the MSI Claw gave me a good excuse to start again. It looks fantastic, and the movement and combat work really well on a controller. I ended up getting into the game rather than constantly thinking about the hardware. When the testing was done, I kept playing.

What is something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

Spending time with Malibu, my Goldendoodle. It’s a good reason to put the computer down for a bit. Otherwise, I enjoy being online. It’s a good way to connect with the world and what interests me. I know a lot of people want to disconnect because the world is stressful, but that’s reality and I like it. I’d rather absorb it all and just make using technology, or being online, a normal thing rather than seeing it as this overarching bad thing that is ruining lives.

Samsung sells a lot of refrigerators. But as reported by Ars Technica (via Star News Korea), a failed firmware update caused some Korean owners’ fridges to “suddenly [lose] power and stop functioning.”

title: Duo-Man turns your 2026 iPhone Duo into a 1980s Sony Walkman
snippet: Long before the iPod, the Sony Walkman was the device of choice for those who wanted to add a soundtrack to their life. Now a Duo-Man app recreates the experience for those of us old enough to have owned one, and you’ll be able to use it with Apple Music … more…
fullText:
Long before the iPod, the Sony Walkman was the device of choice for those who wanted to add a soundtrack to their life. Now a Duo-Man app recreates the experience for those of us old enough to have owned one, and you’ll be able to use it with Apple Music …

Prior to the Walkman, if you wanted to listen to music on the move, your options were limited. Most cassette players of the time were heavy and bulky. When Sony took an audio recorder designed for journalists and shrunk it into the smallest possible cassette player, it quickly became an iconic product.

Developer Vidit Bhargava created the app at a hackathon – and given that many of those present would never have seen one, he brought along the real thing to show them what it looked like.

Duo-Man offers the complete walkman experience on the iPhone Duo. Open the Duo to pick and 'insert' the cassette, Close the Duo to start listening.

Yes, I actually recorded the button clicks and static noise from a real Walkman!

It was fun making this at @bitrig hacks today. pic.twitter.com/juSrLhofrH

— Vidit Bhargava (@viditb) September 27, 2026

You open the Duo, choose your album to insert the tape, and then close it to play.

Bhargava said he originally only created it as a demo app for fun, but will now be releasing it as an actual app. The best comment in the X thread is this one, an image that will only make sense to people of a certain age.

title: Google Pixel 2 XL set the stage for a decade of ups and downs
snippet: Google Pixel’s 10-year anniversary has me taking a look back at a bunch of the milestones throughout this lineup’s history and, when picking up the Pixel 2 XL, hindsight really kicked in as to how this phone was very much a sign of the tumultuous roller coaster that would become Google Pixel. more…
fullText:
Google Pixel’s 10-year anniversary has me taking a look back at a bunch of the milestones throughout this lineup’s history and, when picking up the Pixel 2 XL, hindsight really kicked in as to how this phone was very much a sign of the tumultuous roller coaster that would become Google Pixel.

The original Google Pixel hit the ground running and really did a great job pitching itself. A stellar camera was the main selling point, but Google’s thoughtful software, well-designed hardware, and ecosystem as a whole filled in the bigger picture to deliver a product that, outside of minor gripes, was about as “perfect” as you could ask for from an initial debut in a product category.

Fast-forward to a year later and, oof.

The Pixel 2 and Pixel 2 XL both arrived with some welcome upgrades across the board, but it was also abundantly clear that Google made some serious missteps. The smaller Pixel 2 was a tame revision in basically every way and, outside of the mega-thick bezels, was still a perfectly fine phone.

	

Pixel 2 XL, though, had some glaring flaws.

While I can look back fondly now on many aspects of the Pixel 2 XL, it’s wild in hindsight that a company at Google’s scale, even nearly a decade ago, made such a massive blunder. The Pixel 2 XL’s overall hardware stuck the landing. The updated dual-tone design still has that iconic “Panda” look and the colorful accent button that lived on through prior generations, but the glaring flaw on this device was the display. 

The LG-made panel was horribly inconsistent. In the best-case scenario, you’d get a panel with not-great viewing angles, slightly off colors, and burn-in issues. Worst case, a panel with a blue tint, black smears, and/or a grainy look. I still remember feeling like it was playing the lottery with buying this device and exchanging it to get a “good” one. Google tweaked this over time with software as well as by upping the warranty coverage, but it was still a huge problem with an otherwise great design.

And, in hindsight, that was kind of a signal of what was to come for Pixel as a whole.

	

The Pixel 2 XL tried something new and ultimately fell short, leading to a big correction the following year. Pixel 3 had a stunning display by comparison, and even to this day, Google has invested heavily in giving its phones some of the best displays you can find. The same pattern has been found throughout the lineup. New swings lead to new problems, with Google ultimately scrambling to make the best of it through software updates and making corrections later on. A similarly big problem came with 2020’s Pixel 6 series, with the modem in the first Tensor chip being truly terrible, but Google working to make the best of it in later software updates, only to iterate on the modem with each new generation to the point where, today, Tensor’s modem is roughly on par with anyone else in the ways that matter most.

Google Pixel remains a series that delivers ups and downs through each new generation, but it’s also clearer that the company has finally settled into something that works in 2026. Where the Pixel 2 XL was still in an era where Google would pivot on a whim, the Pixel 11 series comes from a place of stability, predictability, and at least mild success.

title: Vivo X Fold 6 skips the wide form factor, but will launch globally with strong cameras
snippet: Vivo’s new X Fold 6 doesn’t join in on the wide foldable trend, but it has some pretty wild camera promises. more…
fullText:
Vivo’s new X Fold 6 doesn’t join in on the wide foldable trend, but it has some pretty wild camera promises.

The Vivo X Fold 6 packs a punch with an 8.02-inch inner display, a 6.51-inch outer display, and is running on a MediaTek Dimensity 9500 Super Edition chip. That’s with 12GB or 16GB of RAM and 256GB, 512GB, or 1TB of storage.

The cameras are perhaps the biggest standout here, though, as foldables usually have to make some serious compromises in that department. 

The main camera is a 200MP Samsung HPB Large Sensor backed up by a 50MP 3x periscope shooter and a 50MP ultrawide. Everything uses ZEISS imaging and Vivo has a teleconverter add-on to extend the range of the camera. Vivo also says to expect a more responsive shutter and improvements to portrait mode and subject tracking.

	

Rounding out the package is a 6,900 mAh battery, IP58/59 dust and water resistance, and Android 17-based OriginOS 7 out of the box. 

Vivo has confirmed the X Fold 6 will see a global debut though, as always, don’t expect a US release.

title: Motorola’s wide Galaxy Z Fold 8 competitor might be very tiny and called ‘Razr Flex’
snippet: According to a new leak, Motorola’s upcoming entry in the wide, book-style foldable space may be called “Razr Flex” and pack some very familiar specs. more…
fullText:
According to a new leak, Motorola’s upcoming entry in the wide, book-style foldable space may be called “Razr Flex” and pack some very familiar specs.

Specs for Motorola’s wide foldable were shared by Android Headlines alongside a possible name for the device – “Razr Flex.” That’s apparently the name being used internally around the device, so it’s unclear if that would be used as a consumer-facing name. The codename is “Parker,” the report claims.

Much more interesting are the details around the side of this foldable, which shares the same general form factor as Samsung’s smash hit Galaxy Z Fold 8, just in a much smaller footprint. Apparently, the outer display is just 4.97-inches in size – the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is 5.5-inches – while the inner display is less than 7-inches across. Very tiny by modern phone standards, even in this new form factor.

The leaked specs include:

	

4.97-inch outer display (1736×1140)

6.92-inch inner display (2364×1728)

110x149x5.8mm unfolded | 110x76x12.6mm folded

215g

Snapdragon 8 Gen 5

12GB RAM

256GB of storage

5,000 mAh battery with Qi2 (magnets unclear)

IP48/49

50MP main/50MP ultrawide rear cameras, 32MP selfie cameras

PANTONE Coriander, PANTONE Dark Botanical Garden

It’s important to stress just how much smaller this is compared to other wide foldables. iPhone Duo is thicker and heavier than Samsung’s phone, but has roughly the same screen sizes. The closest comparison is the Xiaomi 18 Fold, which has a 5.38-inch outer display, but even that still has a 7.58-inch inner panel. 

The specs are otherwise pretty familiar to the full-size Razr Fold that launched earlier this year.

Concept renders were also shared, but they’re explicitly not based on, well, anything except sketches and Motorola’s general design language – take them not just with a grain of salt, but maybe a whole container.

The “Razr Flex” is said to be launching this year with a “mid-December” debut mentioned.

title: Pixel Buds app update lets Gemini control audio and settings
snippet: With the Pixel 11 launch, Google promised a big Pixel Buds update in September. We’re now starting to see Gemini audio controls with the latest Pixel Buds companion app update. more…
fullText:
With the Pixel 11 launch, Google promised a big Pixel Buds update in September. We’re now starting to see Gemini audio controls with the latest Pixel Buds companion app update.

After updating to version 1.0.981607934 of the Pixel Buds app, we’re seeing @Pixel Buds in Gemini as the latest Connected App. You can control “settings like EQ preset, ANC mode, conversation detection, and touch controls.”

Hey Google, turn up the bass

Hey Google, turn on noise cancellation

This brings up the Gemini overlay, with a “Connecting to Pixel Buds” message appearing along with verbal confirmation.

On devices without the app update, those commands just open the system Bluetooth settings page.

	

We’re seeing Pixel Buds 1.0.981607934 widely rolled out via the Play Store today.

The three other features Google previewed presumably require a firmware update. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 will get Dynamic ANC that adjusts to “compensate when subtle shifts in the seal happen,” like if the buds move in your ear. There’s also Pixel Watch sleep sync that pauses music, disables touch controls, and silences notifications on the Pixel Buds. Finally, you will be able to trigger Live translate by tapping your Pixel Buds.

title: How to Split the Dinner Check With Apple Wallet in iOS 27
snippet: You can now create a Wallet card from a physical business card, and quickly split the bill by scanning a receipt.
fullText:
It’s always fun to dine out with friends, until you have to split the bill. Even if everyone’s willing to pay their share, it can be a headache to figure out who owes what. Fortunately, Apple Wallet in iOS 27 has a new feature that lets you split the bill from a camera image of a receipt.

The feature uses Apple Intelligence to make items on the receipt selectable so you can quickly determine what’s yours (and not yours) and what’s owed. It’s one of several new Wallet features that Apple previewed at its annual software event, WWDC, back in June, that are now rolling out. Those new features include being able to create custom Wallet items from scanned physical cards or from scratch, and view recurring payments if you have an Apple Card.

For iOS 27, Apple also announced new features for developers geared to Apple Wallet, including the ability to make posters for multiticket events and adding order tracking for retail apps using Apple Intelligence.

			

More from CNET

How to use the new check-splitting feature

Before you can take advantage of some of these new Wallet features, you’ll need to make sure your device is using iOS 27.

New iOS 27 Wallet features include the ability to scan a receipt and then split the bill with others.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Receipt splitting in Wallet starts with using the new Siri mode in the Camera app. If you’re pointing your lens at a receipt, a prompt for Split Bill With Apple Cash will come up. You can go through your contacts to search for people you want to split the check with, but they’ll need to be able to pay with Apple Cash. 

Apple Wallet will show a list of the items ordered, and you can select from that list, then choose how you want the bill split and how much to tip. Apple Wallet can’t force your friends to pay; it’s not a collection agency.

How to use the new custom Wallet items feature

To add a Wallet item from a business card, or just create a digital Wallet card without one, tap the plus icon at the top to add something new.

You’ll have the option to scan a debit, credit, transit or other type of ID card, or you can choose Create a Pass to work off a business card.

CNET Senior Writer and iOS features expert Zachary McAuliffe said this feature has already worked well for him. 

Apple Wallet now allows you to create digital passes from physical cards in iOS 27.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

“I digitized my gym membership card, and it’s worked great,” McAuliffe said. “I was worried the scanner wouldn’t pick up my iPhone’s screen, but the scanner seemingly picks up my screen better than my old card. I also appreciate how this saves me space on my already crowded keyring.”

Editing the details of a custom Wallet card allows you to either import the contents of a scanned card and edit them, or just enter your own details. Apple Wallet offers a few different templates for custom Wallet items, and you can adjust the color or background. Item details can be edited later if the information changes or you make a mistake. Newer Apple Watch models should be able to pin these custom digital passes using the Smart Stack feature.

To view recurring payments on your Apple Card, just tap on the Card in Wallet and use the three dots on the top right to select it from the menu.

More iOS 27 Wallet features are likely to roll out as Apple continues releasing updates to its new operating system.

title: The Googlebook marketing push starts with Henry Cavill and his mustache
snippet: Ahead of next month’s launch, Google is beginning the marketing push for Googlebooks with Henry Cavill. more…
fullText:
Ahead of next month’s launch, Google is beginning the marketing push for Googlebooks with Henry Cavill.

The company announced today that it partnered with actor and tech enthusiast Henry Cavill to “help showcase the potential of this next-generation laptop.” Google is specifically referring to “unique software experiences like Continue on phone syncing, Rambler speech-to-text, Antigravity and so much more.”

Cavill, who is a big PC gamer, uses an Android phone. He previously used Pixel phones, with the last appearing to be the Pixel 5, while he was most recently spotted with a Galaxy S25 Ultra.

Google is very much leaning into that: “We recently met with Henry to discuss his own creative ambitions and the conversation quickly turned to the need for a laptop that could keep up with him and work seamlessly with his Android phone.”

	

The premise of this marketing campaign is that Henry Cavill will use a Googlebook to “build a video game.” He’s seen using the HP Googlebook 14 today.

“When Google reached out to me and explained what they are doing with Googlebook, and all of its new, integrated tools, it had me intrigued. So, I asked for the opportunity to have a play with it ahead of release. After being hands on and spending some time with their team, I believe this has the potential to be the start of something rather special. Time and technology are marching forward at a breakneck pace, this, and all that Google are trying to do with it, has the whispers of the next generation.”

—Henry Cavill

This passion project will get underway in November, with @Android on Instagram providing updates, while there’s now a dedicated page: googlebook.google/henry-cavill.

More broadly, Google heavily advertising Googlebooks will be key to its success and this is definitely a start. Hopefully, this will be followed by traditional online and TV campaigns.

title: Reminders just got more powerful, here’s what’s new in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 adds new features to Apple Notes, Messages, Wallet, and more, and it has a few improvements for the Reminders app too. Here’s everything new for Reminders in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 adds new features to Apple Notes, Messages, Wallet, and more, and it has a few improvements for the Reminders app too. Here’s everything new for Reminders in iOS 27.

#1: Describe your reminder

Reminders has offered some level of natural language support for new reminders for a while. But in iOS 27, Apple Intelligence upgrades the feature.

When creating a new reminder, type everything out in natural language and when you type certain info, like a due date, the keyboard row will suggest adding that date to the reminder.

Some basic version of this was available before, but Apple Intelligence makes it more accurate and provides more options than before. Per Apple:

Describe a New Reminder: Use your own words to describe a reminder and Apple Intelligence will help create it for you.

This ‘Describe’ functionality now extends to the reminder detail screen too, letting you jot down your reminder and have it automatically adopt all of the relevant metadata you mention. 

Every time you add or edit reminders inside a list, iOS 27 upgrades the experience with more tools conveniently accessible than before.

In iOS 26, when creating or editing a task you would see five options above the keyboard row: Date, Location, Tag, Flag, and Camera.

In iOS 27, Reminders moves all metadata options into a new box that surrounds your active reminder. And it’s far more robust, with the new UI letting you modify the following:

Date

Time

Urgent

Repeat

Location

Tag

Flag

Camera

You can still tap the ‘i’ icon to view the full set of metadata options, but with iOS 27 you shouldn’t have to do that nearly as often.

#3: Grocery list improvements

Apple says that Reminders’ grocery list auto-sorting feature has been made better in two ways:

it now “sorts grocery list items more accurately”

and grocery list sorting expands to multiple languages

Essentially, due to the more powerful Foundation Models in iOS 27, this feature that’s been around a while is going to work better than ever.

More info on Reminders’ grocery list feature is available here.

title: Big Tech Meets Death in a Hilarious Anti-Enshittification Ad
snippet: Cory Doctorow and a Norwegian nonprofit are behind a comically dark campaign about how everything’s getting worse.
fullText:
Imagine, if you will, a pale figure of Death, dressed in a black robe holding a scythe, alongside a handsome, lumberjack-looking Nordic fella who goes by the name Enshittificator. As partners in crime, they conspire to make your life suck, all because they have the power to make digital products and services worse. 

If that piques your interest — and maybe sounds too much like real life — a recent “anti-enshittification” ad campaign is worth a few minutes of your time.

The term “enshittification” was popularized in 2022 by author and activist Cory Doctorow, and its massive cultural surge earned it a place in Merriam-Webster’s slang hub last year. Enshittification is a deliberate process, designed by companies to maximize profit. 

			

More from CNET

It starts with luring you to a product or service, then making it so good that you become completely dependent on it. The next step is to pull the rug out from under you by hiding basic features behind a paywall, reducing overall quality and squeezing you for every last dime while providing as little value as possible. 

The Death and Enshittificator video above, released on YouTube in mid-September, is the second of a series from the Norwegian Consumer Council, an independent, government-funded nonprofit that advocates for consumer rights. The main character, the Enshittificator, is a bearded Nordic man who says in the first video, released in February, that his “job is to make things shitty.” 

The initial video concludes with Mr. Enshittificator getting into a car accident because he didn’t pay a subscription for his braking system, a scenario he appeared to find amusing. In the second video, he meets Death in the hospital, and the two enter into a business relationship. (He now dons a yellow hazmat suit to stay alive.) 

The duo spends time making every conceivable product worse, from TVs and toothbrushes to smartphone storage. They point out that products with long lifespans, like the famously indestructible Nokia 3310 — which makes a cameo appearance — only generate revenue once. If companies want a profitable business model, however, they have to use low-quality materials, ensure products can’t be fixed and stop issuing updates. 

“Look at all the companies that used to make solid products,” the Enshittificator said. “Where are they now?”

“Dead,” Death said, and they share a knowing smile. 

The Norwegian Consumer Council’s ads are part of its Breaking Free initiative, a multipronged policy approach to make technology work in favor of consumers, rather than against them. The campaign craftily relies on dark humor to detail how enshittification affects everyday life, from paid subscription models to planned obsolescence, which forces you to buy newer devices. 

“The term is often used about digital services that gradually become less useful and more commercial,” an NCC representative told CNET in an email. “But the same feeling applies more broadly: Products that break down too soon cannot be repaired or stop working because support disappears. People recognize the experience immediately.”

It’s true. The videos are also a strikingly accurate commentary on the dismal state of products and gadgets in the digital age. The NCC told CNET that more videos are on the way, but they can’t promise they’ll be in the same universe featuring the same characters. 

Doctorow himself collaborated with the nonprofit to help launch the series, which he’s immensely pleased with. In an email to CNET, he said, “The idea that firms’ market power means that they can worsen their offerings with impunity, combined with the minor license to vulgarity of my dirty little word, have proven a winning combination for helping people direct their anger in the right direction.”

Real life (and death)

It would not be shocking if there were actual boardrooms that looked like this.Norwegian Consumer Council

The enshittification process is relatable and real. In 2020, Apple agreed to pay up to $500 million to settle the landmark “batterygate” class action lawsuit over allegations that it secretly slowed down older iPhone models through software updates. Powerful tech companies have poured massive amounts of money into lobbying against right-to-repair laws, preventing customers from fixing their own devices when they break.  

“It’s really important that the products can’t be fixed,” said the Enshittificator. “It breaks, then it dies, so you have to buy a new one. And another one. And another one. And another one. And another one.”

“This way, we’re actually slowly killing the planet as well,” a smiling Death said, helpfully chiming in. 

The videos also satirize how digital services slowly degrade over time. In one scene, the Enshittificator tells an employee, “The 1,000 pictures of your deceased mother are mine, and you’re going to pay for them.” It’s a direct nod to Google Photos’ 2021 policy shift, which ended free unlimited storage and capped free accounts at 15GB, requiring users to get a subscription to keep already uploaded photos on the platform. 

Another scene takes a jab at automakers who sell you basic functionality as an add-on subscription service. 

“I don’t have any more money. You have me in the palm of your hand,” said the Enshittificator in a fake presentation about selling cars. “You can crush me. So what do you do? Updates. Radio? Premium feature. Heating? Premium feature. Now I have a shitty car, and I can’t afford a new one, but what I can afford is a small monthly payment!”

This is a reference to BMW’s controversial microtransaction model, where it tried to make heated seats and other in-car features part of a subscription plan. While intense consumer backlash forced the German automaker to walk back some of the “add-ons,” several features remain behind a paywall. Other brands have followed suit — Hyundai’s BlueLink and Kia Connect require paid plans to use remote start. For a period, both manufacturers even omitted the remote-start button from the physical key fob, completely blocking owners from using the feature for free.

Can it be fixed?

It’s important, though a little depressing, to imagine how much better life would be if companies actually invested money into making their products better, safer and longer-lasting — and not just more profitable for them. 

An NCC representative told CNET that public response to the ad campaign has been remarkable, with the latest video reaching millions of views in a few days. “What matters most to us, though, is not the views themselves, but that people engage with the reports and policy proposals behind the campaigns.”

In its Breaking Free: Pathways to a Fair Technological Future report, the NCC argues that major tech business models “are often fundamentally incompatible with consumer and human rights.” To dismantle the “walled gardens run by Big Tech feudalists” and end dependence on Big Tech, the nonprofit is pushing for policy reforms built around a three-pronged strategy based on democratic values and principles of openness. 

The first is interoperability, which would force platforms to interface with one another. This is already taking shape under the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required Apple to allow third-party app stores and mandated Meta to support external chats in WhatsApp, 

Next comes portability, which would allow users to move their contacts, content, photos and anything else to rival services. A subscriber fed up with Spotify adding AI features, for instance, would be able to switch to YouTube Music or Apple Music without losing their saved playlists, thereby eliminating platform lock-in. 

Arguably, the most difficult to implement is decentralization of social media, which could shift social media away from single-entity corporate control toward open networks like the Fediverse (which powers platforms such as Mastodon). Though still evolving as protocols develop, decentralization enhances interoperability, making cross-network movement frictionless.

The NCC also told CNET that there are immediate actions Norway (and other countries) can take, such as lowering the VAT (value-added tax) on repair materials, extending consumer claim periods and holding international e-commerce platforms to the same regulatory standards as local businesses.

Reining in Big Tech remains an uphill battle, but in the meantime, the campaign offers a hilarious — and painfully accurate — look at the modern digital hellscape.

“The true mark of success for a project like this is when other people pick it up and run with it,” Doctorow said.

title: Nothing Headphone (1) Pro are $399 with better hardware, ANC, and audio upgrades
snippet: Nothing is today introducing its new Headphone (1) Pro over-ear headphones which deliver hardware improvements, better ANC, and deeper control over how you can tune the final output. more…
fullText:
Nothing is today introducing its new Headphone (1) Pro over-ear headphones which deliver hardware improvements, better ANC, and deeper control over how you can tune the final output.

Following up on last year’s Nothing Headphone (1), the new Pro model brings upgrades across the board. That includes the physical hardware, which is a tiny bit lighter at 327g, while also getting softer ear cups, a wider headband, and thicker padding throughout. The design is also updated with a cleaner look and subtler accents, as well as glass in place of the previous plastic portions.

The biggest upgrades here are the ones that power the audio, though.

Nothing Headphone (1) Pro gets a triple-driver design that provides not only better audio quality, but far more control and flexibility throughout the tuning. In the Nothing X app you get a more advanced custom EQ interface with the option to independently adjust the main drivers and the third “precision driver.” You can get into the weeds of every little detail of the audio here, and it’s far more advanced even compared to the rest of Nothing’s audio gear.

	

Nothing built out the audio experience here with the help of Metropolis Studios, and Headphone (1) Pro also offers a physical switch to let you quickly jump to a “Flat” EQ for a completely neutral sound profile. There are also several presets for Spatial Audio that simulate listening locations such as “Live House,” “Concert Hall,” and more, with head tracking optional.

Active Noise Cancellation is also boosted here, hitting 46 dB, up from the 42 dB on Headphone (1). Nothing says this is through a 10-mic system and a stronger sound seal from the new earcups. 

Like on Headphone (1), Pro supports lossless audio over USB-C while supporting Hi-Res wireless playback as well. You also still get the same plethora of physical controls across the side including the paddle and wheel. 

I’ve been using Nothing Headphone (1) Pro for a few days and, while it’s too early to make a full verdict, there are meaningful improvements throughout, including the much more comfortable hardware. The sheer number of options around tuning the sound quality borders on overwhelming, so I’m still figuring out exactly how I like to listen.

Nothing Headphone (1) Pro will be available starting tomorrow, September 29, at Nothing’s website, Amazon, and Best Buy.

title: MagSafe Monday: Pioneer joins the MagSafe accessory market with the SDA-SC600
snippet: The Pioneer brand is one I’ve trusted for car accessories since Y2K was a concern. I loved their audio gear in my younger days. Pioneer’s SDA-SC600 aims to bring that kind of trusted quality to a MagSafe car mount, bringing Qi2 wireless charging and a built-in fan. more…
fullText:
The Pioneer brand is one I’ve trusted for car accessories since Y2K was a concern. I loved their audio gear in my younger days. Pioneer’s SDA-SC600 aims to bring that kind of trusted quality to a MagSafe car mount, bringing Qi2 wireless charging and a built-in fan.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Pioneer’s SDA-SC600 is a MagSafe air vent mount that holds your iPhone for maps, calls, Siri, etc, and Pioneer also includes a metal ring in the box so non-MagSafe iPhones and Android devices can still mount and use MagSafe technology .

The Pioneer SDA-SC600 is Qi2-compatible, which is almost the latest standard (Qi2.2). Car chargers have historically been one of the weaker links in the MagSafe ecosystem, often topping out well below what you’d get from a wired charger. Qi2 is what you need to ensure a GPS navigation device doesn’t drain faster than you can charge it.

The fan is key in hot climates

Fast MagSafe charging generates heat, which can pose a challenge depending on your climate. Especially right now, I get into my car on 95-degree days, and it’s blistering inside. Pioneer’s integrated cooling fan is built specifically to fight this heat, forcing a slower charge. If you live somewhere with real summers, this is essential for a MagSafe car charger. Pioneer also lists the SDA-SC600 as temperature-resistant more broadly, so it’s built to hold up in extreme cabin conditions at both ends of the weather extremes.

Pioneer also added subtle RGB lightning for as something to set itself apart from other chargers. In the box, you get the mount itself, the air vent adapter, the metal ring for non-MagSafe devices, and a USB-C to USB-C cable to power charger/

Wrap up on Pioneer SDA-SC600

Overall, the Pioneer SDA-SC600 is a solid option for a MagSafe car charger. The light is a nice touch. It supports modern speeds and the fan should keep it cool. The light is a nice touch at night as well.

You can pick up the new Pioneer SDA-SC600 from Amazon or directly from Pioneer.

title: Microsoft Windows and Surface Event: What We Expect to See on Oct. 7
snippet: No, we’re not expecting Windows 12. But we could get a release date for the Surface Laptop Ultra.
fullText:
Microsoft is doing its first dedicated laptop event in two years to present the latest from Windows and Surface devices on Wednesday in San Francisco. This is everything we’re expecting to see – and no, sorry, Windows 12 is not on the list.

The event will be a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC,” according to Microsoft. That makes sense as Microsoft has been all-in on AI by incorporating Copilot everywhere and partnering with chip makers like Qualcomm to bring enough firepower to its devices to handle the computational load of generative and agentic AI tasks. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and the head of Windows and Devices, Pavan Davuluri, are slated to speak.

This event could be when Microsoft actually drops the Surface Laptop Ultra, a 15-inch high-end variant first announced this spring at Computex. The Ultra is powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip, so Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s slated appearance at the event is another sign toward the Ultra. 

			

More from CNET

We already got two new Surface laptops this month, previewed at Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit. At the Hawaii event, Microsoft upgraded its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface 13-inch laptops, running on Snapdragon Elite X2 chips, and introduced a new Surface mouse to go along with them. The new laptops have better cameras and “embody the PC-phone marriage Qualcomm promised years ago,” CNET’s David Lumb reports.

A big question will be prices. Computer hardware companies have raised their prices across the board, from Apple to Asus and Acer, over the last year to keep up with rising manufacturing costs. AI is at least partially to blame, with advanced chips in hot demand for data centers as well as laptops and phones. Other costs, like price increases in Windows licenses during the manufacturing process, may also be contributing to higher price tags. The result, sometimes called RAMageddon, is that it’s more expensive to buy new devices.

Microsoft’s Windows and Surface event begins at 10 a.m. PT / 1 p.m. ET on Wednesday. It is being held in San Francisco and will be livestreamed on YouTube. CNET will be on the ground to bring you all the latest Microsoft news.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Katelyn Chedraoui
						

						

							Reporter 2						
					

											

								

											Katelyn is a reporter with CNET covering artificial intelligence, including chatbots, image and video generators. Her work explores how new AI technology is infiltrating our lives, shaping the content we consume on social media and affecting the people behind the screens. She graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill with a degree in media and journalism. You can reach her at kchedraoui@cnet.com.

title: Moto Tag 2 for Android Find Hub is back in stock for $20
snippet: The Moto Tag 2 is the product of Motorola playing it safe, and that means the Android Find Hub tracker fits in most tracker accessories on the market, making it a pretty good deal. It’s on sale right now for $19 – 33% off after a time out of stock. more…
fullText:
The Moto Tag 2 is the product of Motorola playing it safe, and that means the Android Find Hub tracker fits in most tracker accessories on the market, making it a pretty good deal. It’s on sale right now for $19 – 33% off after a time out of stock.

The Moto Tag 2 normally sits at $29, and that isn’t a bad deal for a tracker that has UWB and a good battery life. It does operate on a coin cell battery, but the battery lasts a good while – Motorola claims 600+ days.

Right now, though, the Moto Tag 2 is down to $19 while Amazon has a deal running. That’s over a third of the price cut, and it’s available on Amazon. The price only applies to the earth-toned variant. The pink version is marked up, for whatever reason.

If you’re new to Android or Google Find Hub trackers, the Moto Tag 2 is a good place to start. It’s shaped like an Air Tag, and purposefully so. That profile allows it to work with any Air Tag accessory, including bags that have a secret pocket, pet collars, or anything you might not want to lose.

	

We’re not sure when this Moto Tag deal will end, though, because it’s been going on for a little while now. That being said, the tracker has been out of stock for the majority of the time, and now that it’s back in stock, it may very well sell out again soon.

Buy the Moto Tag 2 on Amazon
